IMPOSITION OF TARIFF TO PROTECT CANADIAN APPLE INDUSTRY
speechtext: Does the government intend to protect the Canadian apple industry by the imposition of a tariff equal to the tariff imposed by the United States on the importation of Canadian apples?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: IMPOSITION OF TARIFF TO PROTECT CANADIAN APPLE INDUSTRY
speechtext: No. Although the Government is studying a full range of possible measures which might be adopted to mitigate the effects of the U.S. economic measures on the Canadian economy once their impact is clearly defined, it does not plan to retaliate against the effects of the U.S. surtax on Canadian exports. Recent reports suggest that the United States will implement the last of its Kennedy Round cuts on January 1, 1972; Canadian fresh apples would then enter the U.S. duty free. The U.S. surtax would not then apply to U.S. imports of fresh apples.

Of the two to which I specifically wish to refer, the first has to do with the day care provisions and the second with the averaging provisions. Perhaps, before I forget, I ought to say that on Friday afternoon I went to the airport with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who is probably the biggest booster in this House of the child care provisions and of certain day care laws that she wishes to see introduced. She will not be back until this evening. She went to fly to the sunny west and I went to fly to the gloom, down east, Mr. Chairman.
May I make one or two points with regard to the child care provisions. I suspect that these provisions are nuisance provisions, and that we are really providing for nuisance taxation of those good ladies of the neighbourhood who are going to look after the children while mother or father or both are downtown earning their living. I notice, further, that in this provision the social insurance number is to play a large part with regard to receipts. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that that requirement is an abuse of the use of social insurance numbers as originally introduced in this Parliament. Perhaps hon. members within earshot of my voice will remember the assurance that was given when the social insurance number concept was introduced in Canada. According to my understanding, the number was not to be used for the purposes set forth in this clause. That is, it was not to be used in such a way as to identify somebody with the earning of a particular income. That is one aspect about which I want to ask the parliamentary secretary.
The present President of the Privy Council introduced this concept when he was minister of national health and welfare. Clearly, one or the other of them must answer my question, namely, did Parliament intend when the social insurance number concept was introduced that the number would be used to pin down people with respect to income tax, as now contemplated in the section we are being asked to pass? I am referring particularly to the matter of day care centres. I think that is an important matter. In any event, I make the point that that tax will be a nuisance tax. It is a pin money tax, because here we are talking about people who earn very little income and we are asking them to file income tax returns with respect to [The Chairman.]
the very modest amounts of money that they might earn as babysitters for small children. That, I suggest, is unjust.
Not only is the measure unjust, but it may also tend to defeat existing relationships in this field. If babysitters have to pay some kind of tax, it is obvious that, to meet that extra expense, they will tack on to the babysitting charge what they must pay, so that the cost of looking after small children will go up. This matter also involves Canada Pension Plan payments as well as income tax, since the babysitting service might grow to such proportions that it becomes a business which uses certain facilities. All these things will be involved. Either way, the low income, working mother will lose and the good old babysitter next door will be put to a great deal of nuisance, if I may put it that way. I hope that the parliamentary secretary, who has become a very reasonable fellow as the debate has been progressing and who sees other viewpoints, will take a second look at this section during the adjournment hour.
The other point I wish to deal with concerns the averaging of rising income. One might call these the Gordie Howe provisions. Perhaps, after all, they should not be called that, because Gordie Howe is retired and has gone to whatever sanctuary the Eaton Company can provide. Let us call these the Rusty Staub provisions. Rusty Staub plays in right field for the Montreal Expos. The weakness of this plan, as I see it, is that it only permits the averaging of a rising income, so that while Rusty Staub is in his prime and able to hit ever more home runs and do the brilliant fielding of which he is capable, this measure will bring him some advantage. On the other hand, when Rusty loses the strength of his legs-and I apologize to Mr. Staub for using him as an example, but I think it is better if you pin these things down definitely rather than leaving them up in the air without definite form-and when management starts cutting down on what he receives as take-home pay, this provision will not be to his advantage.
According to my reading of the section, he will not be allowed to average his income so as to offset the tax charged on the non-recurring, large income made in the first years. He would, in short, pay considerably more tax than another taxpayer who has had an identical total income over the five year period. Well, Mr. Chairman, I hope that we manage to strike a blow for those who do not quit when their incomes are on the rise but quit when they find that the game is no longer worth the salary they are paid. I suggest that the issue of averaging is most important; yet we should not confuse rising incomes with increased salaries and emoluments which are bound to be paid as a result of inflation. The day may come when the fellow we are talking about has reached his peak and gone past it. Management may not need to tell him to get out. He himself may know that he cannot bargain for those salaries that he commanded in the best years of his life. The player or actor may still be good enough to take part in his profession. The legs may still be good enough for a game and the acting, though not as good as before, may still be good. The fellow may still carry on for a few more years. I think that fellow also deserves a break. At least he is contributing out of a healthy salary scale. He is contributing more than any rookie who takes his place.

I am not referring to large business. I am referring to a neighbourhood mother who takes a few children into her home and looks after them so that their mothers can go to work. I think we can differentiate between a business proposition and a neighbourhood proposition to earn pin money. I ask the parliamentary secretary to look at that. Then, if we grant an averaging system, we have to grant that those who go up also come down. We must look at that aspect as well.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have it confirmed that payments made under the guaranteed income supplement are not taxable. We also have it confirmed that they are not taxable for the year 1971. This is a welcome change that the government has made. It will solve one of the problems created when War Veterans Allowance recipients were pushed, either in whole or in part off the War Veterans Allowance on to the guaranteed supplement.
There still remains a question which many of us have been asking since June 18. It is this: Why has the government not seen fit to make other changes affecting elderly persons likewise effective January 1, 1971? I refer in par-

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act
ticular, of course, to the increase in the age exemption amount from $500 to $650. I realize that now we are in November the present taxation year is almost over, but even if this bill gets passed this month or some time before Christmas, it will come as a bit of a shock to senior citizens to discover when they make out their income tax returns in April that the returns they make at that time must be on the basis of the old law. It seems to me that just as the government has been willing to make the non-taxability of the guaranteed income supplement apply back to January 1, 1971, it should make the extra exemption retroactive to cover the taxation year 1971.
The second point which comes within the purview of these seven sections is the provision that unemployment insurance benefits paid under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, are taxable. I was a member of the committee which poured over that legislation. I recognize the rationale of granting tax deductibility for payments one makes into the unemployment insurance account and having to pay tax on unemployment insurance benefits if they place one in a taxable bracket, but it does seem to me that this should be put into effect only after things have worked out. Application of the principle should, in my opinion, be postponed. We have already run into a number of anomalies in the Unemployment Insurance Act administration arising mainly from the sudden changeover which took place on June 27 when the new act came into effect. We have come across a great many cases of persons who expected to enjoy a certain benefit but who found they could not obtain that benefit because, for example, they were not unemployed until after June 27. This applies to people who are in receipt of Canada Pension Plan payments, to people who are 70 years of age or older, and so on. This is not directly to the point, Mr. Chairman, but it is related to it. My point is that the sudden change has brought about many anomalies and this is another of them, that people have received less by way of unemployment insurance benefit than they thought they would collect. Some people who believed they would receive payments during the best part of the year got only three weeks. I think it is unfair to add to this unfairness by the application of income tax liability at this point.
I am not now making a plea for cancellation of the decision to apply income tax to unemployment insurance benefits. After all, that battle was fought in the committee. But I am asking the parliamentary secretary to delay the coming into effect of this provision for at least a year until things have sorted themselves out and people in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits are getting them on the basis of a structure which is completely founded on the new act.
I hope I have got my point across. What is happening here is that people are losing out because of the changeover and it is a bit cruel to say that not only should they get less money than they would otherwise have received but that such money as they do get is taxable right away. I would therefore urge that implementation of this part be delayed until at least the end of June, 1972.
The other point on which I should like to comment, among the many subjects to be found in these seven

sections, is the provision for income tax consideration with respect to expenses which a working mother is to be allowed. I might add that if the father is the one who is responsible for the children and has to hire help in looking after them, he is entitled under the terms of the bill to the same assistance as is made available to mothers. The consideration is set out in detail in section 63. As my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kingsway has already pointed out, and as she will do again when she gets back, as announced to us by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants-and I can confirm it-there are some features of this provision which bear looking into. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants has called attention to one of them, namely, that though there will be some tax savings to working mothers, because of all the reporting which has to be done, extra taxes may have to be paid by those who do the kind of work which makes it necessary for working mothers to use their services.
Apart from that, it seems to me the principal criticism I have to make with this provision is the standard type of criticism we make with respect to most tax concessions. The proposal is that the taxpayer should get a tax concession in terms of an exemption amounting to a maximum of $500 a child. There is a limit on this. No matter how many children a mother may have the amount cannot be more than $2,000. Then, there is a further limit. A mother cannot claim by way of expenditure on child care an amount greater than two-thirds of her earned income. It is the old story. A working mother with a low income may find that this does not help her much. There is not much point in my saying that a working mother with a high income would probably be better off because a mother with a high income would probably not be out at work.
What is to be granted to these working women, I might point out, is not $500 in cash; it is not $500 off their income tax, or $500 toward the cost of child care. It is simply an exemption of that amount, and by the time one applies a marginal rate of 20 per cent, say, it does not mean as much as it might otherwise have meant. It seems to me this is another case where the tax credit principle would have been far more appropriate. I do not understand why the government continues to resist this tax credit concept as it has done in all cases as far as earned income is concerned. It is true the principle has been applied to investment income in certain cases. Yet a tax credit is a method whereby one can ensure that those in the lower income brackets can get the amounts they need, that, as a matter of fact, they will receive the same amount, if they spend the dollars, as will those in the higher brackets. I do hope that in the study which will yet be given to this proposal some thought might be directed to the application of the tax credit method.
Mr. Chairman, I think that is enough comment on these sections for the time being. We shall be back later.

My hon. friend next to me, in his eagerness to hear what I have to say, almost upset the water, Mr. Chairman. I have a serious proposition to put before the parliamentary secretary. I have discussed it briefly with him and he promised to respond to any submission the opposition might make with regard to it. It has to do with the proposed taxation of scholarships, fellowships and bursaries. Research grants, Canada
November 1, 1971

Council grants and similar grants will be taxable, and the cost of equipment, fees, travel, lab charges, etc., will be deductible. In commenting on this section I should like to remind the committee that at present such bursaries and scholarships are exempt from tax. The change in the legislation will mean a reduction in income, particularly for graduate students. The provinces' efforts to maintain graduate schools and to compete with attractive scholarship programs in United States universities will only be weakened. Furthermore, students will be able to obtain United States scholarships tax free. In a country like ours which is not comparatively generous with graduate students in general and with their activities, I suggest with great respect this proposal is a retrograde one. If one goes back to the Carter Commission, one learns that this commission maintained that one of the strategic sources of economic growth is a rapid improvement in the educational quality of the labour force. That is really part of the thrust or one of the many aspects of the report with which we have to deal.
The new legislation we are considering not only imposes an extra burden on young students but also on university professors who are receiving grants to conduct research that is essential to their respective fields. By taxing scholarships, fellowships and bursaries with only a $500 exemption, the minister has completely reversed the direction in which the Carter Commission said that tax reform should move. This proposed change will mean that the provinces' efforts to maintain graduate schools and to compete with attractive scholarship programs in United States universities will be seriously hamstrung. I am making this appeal to all members of this committee, no matter what their political persuasion may be, who have an interest in university and graduate school work and in the essential part that this plays in our country. Fellowships are traditionally granted to Ph.D. level graduate students who are engaged in research.
Sabbatical leave at most universities is granted at about 50 per cent of full salary. This means that through careful planning, with perhaps the addition of a research grant, a teacher may be able to move himself and his family abroad in order to consult resource material essential to his field. I suggest the government has not given sufficient consideration to the hardship its proposal will create for those academics who have planned to spend the academic year 1971-72 on sabbatical leave abroad. In other words, midway through their term-a term that has nothing to do with the enactment of this bill-there is to be a major change in taxation for recipients of bursaries and fellowships. From September to December they are not taxable; from January to the end of their year, to put it very simply, they will be taxable should this bill get the approval of Parliament.
The government plans to implement its proposals for taxation of non-residents on income from a Canadian source a couple of months hence, namely by January 1, 1972. I earnestly suggest that even if the bill cannot be changed now, or if the government does not see the merit of my comments, there should be some transitional arrangements for students who are well along in their sabbatical year or their year of research. For those who
Income Tax Act
have already made their arrangements and are now out of the country or about to leave with grants awarded from six months to a year ago, the action the government is taking will almost certainly result in their having to curtail their stay, and consequently their research, unless additional funds are made available to them. It seems to me paradoxical that a government that is anxious to promote excellence, and which has recently appointed a minister of science and technology to look into this and other elements in this field, should narrow the base, so to speak, of taxing proposals which will have a serious effect on our whole graduate student program.
It seems to me strange that the minister has made transitional periods available for such industries as mining and petroleum, as well as the transitional period for corporation income tax which has been written into the act. Just the other day we had the minister's amendments to the co-operatives and caisse populaire provisions, yet the area concerning me at the moment has apparently been disregarded. I suggest that the graduate program is of equal validity in the argument for flexibility of approach upon the part of the government. A transitional period of at least six months until July 1, 1972 would enable those teachers committed to spending this academic year pursuing research to do so. When I have finished my remarks in a minute or so I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to state that a transitional period will also be effective for this vital element in our nation's wealth.
The most ridiculous aspect though of the new legislation is that which governs moving expenses as applied to persons undertaking a year of research work outside Canada. An individual is allowed to deduct the cost of moving his family abroad to complete a specific research project. But once the project is completed, the current legislation does not allow this individual to deduct the cost of returning his family to Canada-I am sure there is a mistake here, and if there is I shall be glad to hear the parliamentary secretary admit it-since his research project has been completed and, by law, he is allowed no further deductions. It seems that the minister is not only attempting to discourage students from completing then-education in Canada through his tax on scholarships and bursaries, but he is attempting to keep young Canadians out of their country permanently. I am sure that this cannot be the intention of the minister, despite the rather loose construction of the statute, and I shall be glad to hear that I am wrong on this issue. A man undertaking a year of research work outside the country surely is entitled to deduct the cost of taking and returning his family.
The Official Opposition suggests that this should be clearly stated, in view of the fact there is no relief provided under section 62 for moving expenses. A man is entitled to a one-way cost deduction within Canada if moving to take up new employment, and that is all. Obviously, an academic on research leave does not qualify here since he may not be "a student in full time attendance at an educational institution". The new legislation should be more specific, I suggest, and should include a provision for those on extended research leave to deduct the cost of moving their families; for example, "a scientist, a teacher or other researcher engaged in research which requires

Income Tax Act
his continued absence from his normal place of residence".
Under section 56(l)(o) we encounter the problem of matching cash received in the taxation year with expenses incurred in the academic year. I suggest provision should be made in the legislation to permit the holder of a research grant to carry back expenditures in order to match expenses with revenue received in the taxation year. I presume that this is what the department will want to do, but we nevertheless feel that it should be clearly spelled out at this stage of the legislation. In the matter of short-term employment, defined as anything less than the full academic year of any institution, that is summer school, guest lectureships and so on, universities have traditionally not provided a special travel grant. The individual has been defined as having employment status within the second institution and has been ineligible to deduct these travel expenses to and from that institution. A teacher engaged in short-term employment should have the right to deduct the cost of travel to and from his employment.
I hope this point will be clarified quite quickly by the parliamentary secretary, and perhaps the other points I have raised can be cleared up so the whole philosophy, which I should think the government would support enthusiastically, that is the philosophy and importance of not hamstringing our program of graduate research, will not be modified by taxation proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to rise to support the persuasive words the hon. member for Fundy-Royal has just put to us. He has made a general case in respect of professors and students, and, while I would agree with everything he has said, I would add a few other considerations.
It seems to me that the problem in respect of section 56(1), paragraphs (n) and (o) is a classification problem, and is a difficult problem in the academic world itself. I do not know of any sharp distinction which is made in the academic world between concepts such as scholarships, bursaries and fellowships. Even within some universities there seems to be some confusion, and certainly as between universities it would be hard to establish a crystal clear pattern and meaning for them.
It is also important to note that the additional classification which appears in (o), that is, a grant which is to enable one to carry on research or similar work, is not really substantially different or different in kind at all from that of fellowship or scholarship money granted to graduate students across the country. Therefore, it is illogical that in one place you should be allowed more than $500 to be attributed to the expenses one incurs in the pursuit of scholarship or research work, but not in another place.
Therefore I suggest that the words "scholarship, fellowship or bursary" be deleted from paragraph (n) and inserted in paragraph (o). I do not know whether that would leave anything worth retaining in paragraph (n), although I expect that the words "prize for achievement" have a rather different meaning, so that if the parliamentary secretary were disposed to transpose these words

there could be a reason for still retaining paragraph (n). I would strongly urge on him the advisability of using the words "scholarship, fellowship or bursary" in paragraph (o). I also suggest that paragraph (o) might then read, following the words "or in similar work": "or on account of any fellowship, scholarship or bursary". Then, following the word "exceeds" I would suggest the insertion of the additional words "$500 or", which would provide two different methods of dealing with the deduction being claimed. The whole thing would then read:
(o) the amount, if any, by which any grant received by the taxpayer in the year to enable him to carry on research or any similar work or on account of any fellowship, scholarship or bursary, exceeds $500 or the aggregate of expenses incurred by him in the year for the purpose of carrying on the work-
Like the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, I should like to draw the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary to the fact that an injustice is being done to these people in relation to scholarships, fellowships and bursaries this year, or indeed on sabbatical leave during the academic year 1971-72. This year is already in progress and we are proposing, without any transitional period being allowed, to impose this as of January 1.
It may perhaps be thought that this difficulty could be avoided if the granting bodies were prepared to grant the whole of the money before the end of this calendar year. That would certainly avoid the application of the new law. Aside from the fact that universities would probably be reluctant to put themselves in the position of appearing to avoid the payment of tax on part of their faculties by paying earlier, there is also the consideration that many of the granting bodies would certainly not be in a position, for financial or administrative reasons, to advance the date on which they make the second instalment of their funds for the present academic year.
Therefore, just as we have made a transitional period for various business groups under the tax law, I would suggest it would be more than appropriate that there be a transitional period for people involved in this particular field. This is also true of professors on sabbatical leave this year. Although that point arises more properly under section 115,1 believe these people are often geographically far removed from dealing with universities and other granting bodies, and therefore unable to persuade these bodies to pay them the full amount before the end of this year, resolving their problem in that way. Many are probably abroad, and if we enact this legislation just as it is we will place them in a very difficult position this year.
I do not believe there is any great need for me to go through all the other points made by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal. I am in complete agreement with the policy statements and details he has presented. I would merely conclude by urging the parliamentary secretary and, through him, the minister, to give very serious consideration to the points which have been raised.
These young people or young professors who may be taking advantage of the opportunity of furthering their studies, and their own careers as well, by continuing their research are performing a task which is of benefit not only to them but also to the whole country, especially at this time when there are so many cries throughout the country that we should have Canadian professors teaching Canadians. That is not a cause which I thoroughly
November 1, 1971

endorse, and is much overdone from time to time, but we do want to ensure that there is a ready pool of qualified Canadians who could be university professors. We also hope that universities will hire them when their competence and qualifications are equal to those from abroad. If we do not put provisions in our tax laws to ensure this, then the universities and the academic profession in Canada will be the worse for it.

Mr. Chairman, I think I goofed when I spoke earlier about income averaging, which is really not within the group or section with which we are now dealing, so perhaps the parliamentary secretary would be kind enough to forgive me and deal with that during the next round rather than when dealing with this group.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was simply going to respond to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants on that point by suggesting to him that the parliamentary committee wrestled at considerable length, as did the experts retained by that committee, with the whole problem of downward averaging, but no satisfactory solution to that question was found, nor are we aware of any jurisdiction in which a satisfactory answer to the question could be devised and applied. I am not so sure I would have any different or lengthy explanation when we do come to the appropriate section, so I thought I might as well get that off my chest now.
The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants also raised the question of the administrative burden, if you like, being imposed on recipients of payments from the taxpayer, which the taxpayer proposes to deduct under the child care allowance provisions of this bill. I think at first blush one must agree there is an administrative burden imposed here. I would suggest to the hon. member that the absence of provisions such as those to which he has taken exception would create something more like a barn door than a loophole in the Income Tax Act, particularly bearing in mind that payments under that section are allowed to be made to members of the immediate family of the taxpayer. I think equity among all taxpayers rather demands that, as a general principle, where a taxpayer is allowed to deduct from his taxable income some payment he has made there should be a very good reason for not ensuring that it be included in the taxable income of some other taxpayer. Certainly, I can see the administrative difficulty which would be imposed on individual taxpayers by this provision, but I am afraid I have no alternative that would satisfy what I regard to be the basic requirement of the Income Tax Act that we ensure equity between taxpayers and at the same time avoid imposing this particular burden.
The hon. member mentioned the question of the social insurance number as a matter of principle. It is my understanding that at the time that particular law was brought in the then Prime Minister of Canada gave assurance that Canadians would not be required to produce that number. However, it would appear that the undertaking by the former Prime Minister was prempted by the enactment of section 130(A) of the present Income Tax Act. I would refer the hon. member to that particular section which is reflected in section 237 of the bill before us I believe in
Income Tax Act
identical terms, although I have not compared the two verbatim. Section 130(A) was enacted in the 1966-67 session of Parliament and, as I say, would rather overrule Mr. Pearson's commitment.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested, not unexpectedly, that other amendments which would increase exemptions and otherwise lighten the tax burden on our older taxpayers should be implemented with retroactive effect for the current tax year. The tax package as presented to the House in Bill C-259 involves a related grouping of exemptions, of deductions, of income inclusions of allowances and so on and it is certainly not beyond the realm of ingenuity of the government, from a legal point of view, to present it piecemeal, but the fact is that it is not the intention of the government to present it in that way.
I do not think the hon. member is entirely justified in relating these various provisions, such as the increase in exemptions to older taxpayers from $500 to $650 and the reduction of age for that from 70 to 65, to the retroactive exclusion of the guaranteed income supplement for the current tax year. As the hon. member pointed out, the anomaly of the inclusion of part of the guaranteed income supplement payment during the current year was the result of amendments relatively recently adopted by Parliament to the old age security act. Certainly, the government did not intend the result from the income tax point of view which occurred, so we are moving quickly to remove that anomaly for this year. However, I think I must regard the other amendments in Bill C-259 as being part of the over-all reform and not subject to piecemeal implementation.
The hon. member also suggested by way of a transitional period at least that the inclusion of unemployment insurance benefits in taxable income should be deferred. I noted he did not suggest that the deduction of unemployment insurance premiums from taxable income be deferred as well. I think those two items go hand in hand. I again perhaps would lump them in the same general area as the earlier discussion about the treatment of senior citizens. This is a tax reform package and there are numerous changes both in deductions, exemptions and items of accretion to wealth which should be included in taxable income.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville dealt with the problem of taxation in respect of scholarships, fellowships, bursaries and research grants. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal as well as the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville have discussed this with me privately on earlier occasions, although I must say that in speaking to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal I was under the impression that the item we were talking about involved the problem of the professional on sabbatical or otherwise non-resident which really comes up under section 115 rather than under this particular block of clauses with which we are dealing. However, it is a problem of the same nature; at least, it deals with the same group of taxpayers and perhaps it would be appropriate to discuss it here. Section 56 does require that all scholarships, fellowships, bursaries and prizes for achievement in excess of the exemption of $500 be included in income. This $500 exemption is deductible

from the aggregate of those classes of income. That is a point which must be made clear.
It should also be pointed out that while any items of scholarship, bursary, and so on in excess of $500 must be included in income, students are still able to deduct from their total income their tutition fees and in many cases the moving expenses which are incurred as a result of moving to permit them to use the scholarship at a particular institution. They also have their personal exemption. If we take the example of a single student who reeives a scholarship or bursary, he has his $1,500 personal exemption, he has the standard $100 deduction and he has the special $500 deduction. This brings his total deduction to $2,100. Then, on top of that he has the amount if any he pays in tuition fees to the institution he is attending. I do not think in reality anyone could argue that students who are in receipt of scholarships, bursaries and so on are likely to be impoverished as a result of this decision. The decision here was made as a result of the recommendation of the Commons committee. I think we have to make a distinction. I gather from the hon. member for Windsor-Walker-ville that the institution of higher learning have not yet themselves distinguished between research grants, scholarships and bursaries.
The section regarding research grants contains provisions which basically have been in the law before and which allow a taxpayer on receiving a grant to deduct expenses that are incurred by him. I think representatives of universities and graduate schools whom I have met over the past several months have been fair in admitting that there was a bit of a tax dodge here that was being rather well used in certain quarters in respect of research grants for overseas purposes.
The anomaly, as suggested by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, of the moving expenses being allowed to a student or other recipient of a research grant carrying on his work outside Canada when he is moving from Canda to wherever he is doing his research but not back, is based on the principle that the deduction of expenses incurred in earning a research grant must be made against the research grant itself. I would expect that if a student-if I may use that term to include not only students but many professors-goes overseas, conducts his research, exhausts the research grant and decides to stay on with his family for holidays, a pretty good question arises as to why the return fare should be a write-off against the research grant. If, on the other hand, his research grant involves work overseas and work back here in Canada to complete its use, the travelling expenses both ways would undoubtedly be allowed. So, I think there is equity in the provision before us.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville raised in specific terms the problem of those who are currently on a sabbatical or otherwise out of the country. This is a genuine problem. Again, it is a problem that I have discussed with the universities and with graduate school representatives. If for no other reason they needed to know several months ago what our intentions were from their own budgeting point of view. The option is open to them to make the funds available to the student for the balance of the term of his arrangement with them before the end of

this calendar year, and if that is done then of course it will not be taxed as provided in the current act. Other than that there are, I am sure, throughout the whole act, through any major change in the income tax legislation, a number of places where persons may be caused some inconvenience and where indeed they incur some cost as a result of major revisions to the income tax laws. Transitional provisions, such as the hon. member for Fundy-Royal noted, have been afforded to many of our industries, to the co-operatives and credit unions most recently by amendments tabled here. But the point of transitional provisions is to relieve some relatively long term problems that may arise as a result of the new provisions, and certainly not to relieve situations which will resolve themselves in a matter of months, as is the case here.
1 think that deals with all of the questions. I am sorry that my response could not have been more favourable, but if I have missed anything, I am sure hon. members will call it to my attention.

May I just say a further word on this subject, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me that in his discussion regarding moving expenses the parliamentary secretary has been somewhat unfair. It may be, of course, that there are some professors who combine their work with a subsequent European holiday, but this is surely not the rule. I do not know whether it happens as often as it does not, but I think a provision could be written into the act which could take that into account. If it was half play and half work, that would be a different situation from the situation of someone who goes to Europe purely for research purposes and returns here having accomplished his research.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I suppose I will have to ask the hon. member whether he took his wife and family purely for research purposes, because this is the problem we have in these areas. I do not blame a man, from the point of view of his own family life, wanting to take his family with him when he goes away for that long a trip, but much of the travelling expense that is incurred in these cases would in ordinary circumstances be regarded as personal and not incurred for earning an income.
May I ask the parliamentary secretary whether, if the person did not take his family with him, he could then claim expenses both ways.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The Income Tax Act does not envisage in ordinary circumstances, and subject to the special problems mentioned by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the deduction from taxable income of personal living expenses.

I would like to say a few words on section 60 and that portion of subsection (e) dealing with exemptions for university students registered at a recognized college or university here in Canada. Many times in the House I have urged that no income tax should be levied on the earnings of students who are willing to finance their own university education. Perhaps this plea has fallen on deaf ears and I have a suggestion to make to the parliamentary secretary. Under subsection
(e), which deals with tuition fees, the student is granted the privilege of deducting from his taxable income the
November 1, 1971

amount of tuition fees, so perhaps we should give him some other basic deductions here.
In some other sections, certain arbitrary amounts are set which the taxpayer may deduct for specific purposes. Perhaps it would be difficult to set an arbitrary amount to help finance the cost of living away from home, such as residence fees, the cost of textbooks and so on. I wonder what the parliamentary secretary would say to doubling the basic exemption for a single person who is forced to live away from home to obtain his education. All members of the House are continually being asked for assistance by students endeavouring to obtain student loans. It seems to me that doubling their basic exemption while they are registered at a recognized university or college might be a means of doing away with a student loan, the means test that goes with it, and all the administrative detail as well as the disappointment in not getting it. It seems to me that to double the basic exemption of a single person, as I suggested, would make it unnecessary for a student to apply for a student loan. In addition, the summer earnings that he makes would, in a large measure, be his own.
Perhaps this would be one way of assisting our young people to obtain a college education. There may be other ways. The parliamentary secretary may have a better way of assisting these people, but I suggest this off the top of my head as one way of doing it, that is to increase the basic exemption. If doubling it would be too much, we could put in some other figure. I think it is rather contradictory for the government, on the one hand, to provide student loans and, on the other hand, to force these same students to pay income tax on the earnings they have made to finance their education away from home. I think we want to look at another way of doing it, and it could be found by increasing exemptions as I have suggested.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I should like to respond briefly to a couple of the comments the parliamentary secretary made a few minutes ago. He seemed to feel that it was difficult to adjust the income tax package in such a way as to provide for the exemption of the $650. for senior citizens to be made retroactive to January 1, 1971. I am grateful to him for having pointed out to me earlier how the bill deals with the matter of making the guaranteed income supplement not taxable for this year. It is simply a matter of section 71 at page 702 being written into the bill. The changed wording is spelled out and subsection (2) reads:
This section is applicable to the 1971 taxation year.
In other words, what it amounts to is that when the government wants to make a change retroactive rather than in the current year, it seems to have no difficulty in doing it. I continue to express my regret that this change has not been made so that when senior citizens are computing their income tax for the year 1971 they will get the benefit of it. As it stands, they will have to wait until they are computing their income tax for 1972, away off in April, 1973. A lot can happen between now and then.
The other subject which I raised on which the parliamentary secretary was generous enough to make comment was unemployment insurance. The ease with which
Income Tax Act
my friend can brush aside these complaints is something to behold. I know there is income tax deductibility for the few cents that people pay into the unemployment insurance account as opposed to the tax that they have to pay on their benefits. It is almost a one horse-one rabbit situation. Apart from that, I regret to say that the parliamentary secretary seemed to miss my point altogether. I was not arguing the rights or wrongs of permanent basis. What I was pointing out was the the sudden change-over on June 27 has produced many anomalies under which people are getting less than they thought they were going to get, despite all the unemployment insurance commission's advertisements that this new act is such a wonderful deal. I suggest that because these anomalies are having this effect it might be reasonable to request that they be softened by not applying income tax to unemployment insurance benefits for at least a year. I am sorry that the parliamentary secretary misunderstood my point.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question? The hon. member for Lambton-Kent.

Mr. Chairman, while we are on section 56, I should like to direct a simple question to the parliamentary secretary and I think it will only take him a moment to reply. Section 56(C)(ii) mentions retiring allowance. If this is a little honorarium received by an employee on retirement, generally a couple of hundred dollars, that is fine but is there a provision whereby executives are able to take advantage of this retiring allowance in order to receive a fat bonus from their employer? May I ask the parliamentary secretary if there is a ceiling on the amount covered by this item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not quite understand the purport of the hon. member's question. This is not an exclusion or an exemption from income; this is an amount which must be included when computing income for the taxation year. The retiring allowance must be included in income.
I should point out that the option is there, and as we mentioned when discussing the comment made by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants earlier, if the lump sum is very large the taxpayer may opt to purchase an annuity. This would effectively spread the taxation over the period that the annuity was payable rather than it having to be paid in the taxation year the lump sum was received. But the amount is taxable; it is not an exclusion, it is not a loophole or break for anybody.

I am pleased to have an explanation from the parliamentary secretary. However, the section says, "but not including" and then goes on, so it is a classic example of how confusing this bill is to people who are not as skilled as the parliamentary secretary. I shall have to take his word for it.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the parliamentary secretary another question. On page 131, paragraph (j) reads:
amounts that the taxpayer became entitled to receive in the year upon the disposition of an interest in a life insurance policy, to the extent provided by section 148;
At page 408, section 148 (1) (a) reads:
in respect of any life insurance policy other than an annuity contract, the amount, if any, by which the proceeds of the disposition of an interest in the policy that he became entitled to receive in the year exceeds the adjusted cost basis of the policy to the policyholder as of the time of the disposition;
That is not so terribly confusing but paragraph (b) reads:
in respect of any life insurance policy (other than a policy that is a registered retirement savings plan or that is or is issued pursuant to a registered pension fund or plan)-
This is the point that I am a little concerned about, and maybe I shall have to call again on the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre:
-all or any part of the insurer's reserves for which vary in amount depending upon the fair market value of a specified group of assets (in this section referred to as a "segregated fund"), such portion of any amount allocated to the policyholder in the year under the policy as was allocated out of gross revenue of the insurer from the segregated fund, other than gross revenue that is a dividend (other than a taxable dividend) received by the insurer on a share of the capital stock of any corporation.
What happens to the policy holder of a mutual company?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If any amount is allocated to his credit as a result of the policy he holds in the mutual company, I do not think there is any distinction in this particular case between a mutual company and a shareholder owned company. This refers to amounts that are credited to the policy account of a policyholder and, of course, excludes payments made in respect of a policy that is used to implement a registered retirement savings plan, pension fund, and so on. This is simply an accretion of his assets as a result of the holding of his insurance policy. I admit that this is complicated terminology because of the desire to exclude the retirement savings plan and others like it. I just do not know whether I can explain it any better. This is the amount which becomes the property of the taxpayer

during the taxation year as a result of his owning that insurance policy, and it is therefore included in his income.

I thank the parliamentary secretary. What is the segregated fund? I notice that is mentioned here. According to my experience, there is a reserve fund or a reserve with respect to an insurance policy. There is also the dividend that is declared with respect to participating policies. Many people have said that the dividend is merely the refund of an overcharge on the premium. Frankly, this provision is completely confusing. I do not know who understands it. Certainly, I do not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the taxation of insurance companies is a rather specialized subject at best, and I am sure I will be more prepared to deal with it when we come to section 148, although, as the hon. member notes, this subject is brought in, by reference, here.
I am advised that the segregated fund referred to in subparagraph (b) is a very special sort of arrangement. Not all insurance companies have entered into that arrangement. Some do not have segregated funds. The fund may be referred to in this manner: an insurance company may issue a special class of policy with respect to which it sets up a particular reserve that applies to that class of policy but not to all policies which would be in the general reserve. I am afraid I am not able to answer the hon. member's question in a more satisfactory way. The general rule as to what credits to his account or to his policy account the taxpayer has to add to his income is covered in subparagraphs (a) and (b) and relates to exceptional circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be related to life insurance policy proceeds. As my colleague for Lambton-Kent has indicated and as the parliamentary secretary has indicated, this taxation of insurance companies and insurance policies is a new area of taxation and there is a great deal that is hidden. The side note by section 148 merely says, "Subsection 79D(1) modified". That word "modified" is the interesting word. Certainly, there is a considerable spreading out into the field of insurance here. I am wondering what the government's philosophy is in moving in here. Is it doing its best to try to take every dollar it can get and to discourage every form of saving that is made in this country? Canadians as such have a reputation for being strong savers via life insurance. Why the government feels, and I am speaking particularly of this administration, that big brother knows best, I do not know. This administration wants to get every blessed dollar it can and to discourage saving by individuals through life insurance which, in itself, is one of the best sources of domestic investment in this country.
Look at, shall we say, the proportion of Canadians who invest in life insurance and then at the performance of the life insurance companies in investing in Canada; and yet here we are, moving in on people who do not have large incomes and who are not in any privileged position. There is hardly a household today in this country, unless it is a very improvident one, that does not hold some form of life insurance, be it only of some limited kind. It may be only burial insurance. There is some degree of life insurance in almost every household. Yet here we are, as I say, moving
November 1, 1971

in, digging, digging and digging deeper to dissipate and break up the attractiveness of life insurance. And for what purpose? Because big brother government says it wants the money and can spend it better. This is the^ very fundamental philosophy of a government that says, "We need the money and therefore must find it". I say they tax up to their expenditures. I have been saying this for years and years, and that applies particularly to this administration. This process started under the previous administration. They tax right up to their expenditures-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman.
-and they always want more money.
The parliamentary secretary ought to let the hon. member finish his sentence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is a very eloquent speech. Yet I do not think the hon. member ought to leave the impression that these provisions are new in the amending tax bill. These provisions have been carried forward from the existing Income Tax Act. May I remind the hon. member that subsection 56(l)(f) which the hon. member referred to when originally opening this question is similar to a provision presently in the act. The clause which he is excoriating at the present moment is subsection 79(D) of the present Income Tax Act. So, while the philosophy is good and the speech is great, we are really not talking about changes in the income tax law.

Mr. Chairman, that is the type of intervention that comes from the parliamentary secretary. The wording opposite section 148 is, "Subsection 79D(1) modified." If the word "modified" means nothing, take it out. We have seen many areas in which a tax might be modified. There are many things which might slip in under a modification. For instance, you could double a tax as a result of a modification. As I was saying, this administration is moving further and further into the area of taxation of life insurance proceeds and life insurance companies. Surely to goodness it is germane to the thrust of the argument to say what I have said. If the parliamentary secretary wants to say something or argue a point, let him not rise on a point of order, because section 56(j) refers to section 148, and I am talking about section 148. There is no way one can raise a point of order with regard to relevancy of taxation of life insurance proceeds by trying to say this just carries forward an old section of the act. The explanatory note says this is a modification. If the parliamentary secretary wants to embark on how thin his knowledge is, let him indicate precisely in language that can be understood by members how the modification works and how this language is explained. Then, we will agree with him. Let us not take anyone to task about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in response to-
That is all right. I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has invited a comment. When we are
Income Tax Act
dealing in committee with section 148, I will be very pleased to give detailed answers. However, that section is not among the block of sections before us at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I doubt whether that is a point of order. The hon. member for Edmonton West has the floor. He should be allowed to continue his remarks.

If I have to read the words into the record in order to clarify this point, I will do so. Section 56(l)(j) reads:
Amounts that the taxpayer became entitled to receive in the year upon the disposition of an interest in a life insurance policy, to the extent provided by section 148;
No one is going to ask this committee to pass section 56(l)(j) without a reference to section 148. If we did, when we comment on section 148, we would be faced with the argument that it, had already been approved in principle. I do not normally like to be cranky, but this type of intervention does not help the situation one bit. In any event, I made my point. We are moving further and further into the savings of Canadians by these further extensions of taxation of life insurance. If it started to creep in or earlier budgets, there is nothing wrong with commenting on it today. We must cry "halt" to this sort of thing.
I now wish to move beyond section 56 and again make reference to the child care expenses in section 63. If the parliamentary secretary has already made a reference to this, it will be sufficient. I do not know whether he has had an opportunity of discussing with the minister the proposition I put to him the other day about the limitation of age 21 of a relative to whom a payment may not be made. Many provinces have now adopted age 18 for the adult. It seems ludicrous to exclude from this new proposal persons between the ages of 18 and 21.
In addition, persons age 18 earning $600 a year or more from employment are obligated to pay into the Canada Pension Plan. This is one of those types of operations where contributions may have to be made to the Canada Pension Plan by the employer. At today's rates, it certainly does not take much for a full time child care attendant to earn $600 per annum. I do not know of any householder who can get full care for a child or children for less than $50 a month. If that is the case, the parent who hires the child attendant will have to make a contribution to the Canada Pension Plan, and it is necessary to make such a contribution to the Canada Pension Plan for a person between the ages of 18 and 21. Under the Income Tax Act, for certain relatives between the ages of 18 to 21, as proposed in this bill, a working mother will be disentitled to child care allowance because of the reference in this provision to age 21. If he has not already done so, I urge the parliamentary secretary to discuss this matter with the minister to see if we can bring about a little bit of normalcy or uniformity between the Canada Pension Plan requirement and that part of the Income Tax Act relating to child care allowance.
In addition, we will want to say something when section 74 is before the committee and the related questions with regard to the wife as an employee of her spouse's business. I merely want to mention this again. It is highly inequitable for the wife of a country town doctor or den-

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act
tist who must act as a nurse-receptionist in the small clinic where her husband and associates work to be precluded from obtaining the child care allowance, although she, has to go into the clinic in order to utilize her skills or it may be required that she work. It may be said by some that this is not necessary for professionals. What about young professionals trying to establish themselves in a rural town? Such professionals do not earn that much money in the early stages.
It is often necessary for the wife of the doctor or dentist to act as receptionist or nurse. The act disallows her to be classified as a separate wage earner. It disallows her the working mother's entitlement under the amendment to the act. This may be even more important in the case of someone who works for a partnership in which her husband is involved, particularly a non-professional business. If people feel professionals earn enough to get along, that is one way of looking at it. However, I know of many instances of carpenters, plasterers, electricians and others where the wife of a partner or possibly the wives of two partners have to work in the business in order to make a go of it. Under the proposed section 63 of the act, they are disentitled. This is wrong. There is thus a discrimination that should not exist.
It is always very interesting when the general public decides the government has done something popular. In this case, the government is alleged to be allowing working mothers to claim child care expenses. However, if you look at the fine print, you will see that the limitations are rather severe. The wording certainly curtails the scope of this provision of the act. Many people feel that they might qualify, but they will be absolutely astounded when they read all the qualifications. I do not know just how much good this will do.
The other matter I want to deal with is moving expenses. I do not know what can of worms this is likely to open or how many regulations will have to be brought in so as to eliminate abuse. Just how far will taxpayers have to go in order to justify their claim that a move results from a change in employment? Suppose it were a technological change? Some of our larger companies keep several operations going within such cities as Toronto and Montreal and staff are often transferred from one plant to another. Or consider some of our major department stores. In my own city of Edmonton, Woodwards, for instance, have a branch near the northern limits of the city, almost on the border of my constituency. They also have a store about nine miles away as the crow flies, in the southern part of the city. Staff are transferred between one store and the other. It could happen that a member of the staff was promoted, say, from assistant buyer to buyer on condition that he move to the other store. If he lived close to his original place of employment he might well decide that he could not put up with going back and forth across the city to work. So he would sell his home and buy another, or rent an apartment much closer to his new place of work. It is nonsense to insist that a man ought to spend an hour or an hour and a half every day travelling to work and back.
But would the cost of moving be deductible in such a case? Or will the regulations insist that in order to qualify

people must move a distance of at least 25 miles? What are the basic requirements to be? This is what we must consider. Are we thinking in terms only of new work, a new job, a fresh start with a new employer? I know there was a good deal of discussion on this point during the committee hearings. Our conclusions were indefinite. It was a subject which seemed to open up, as I say, a can of worms. I hope the parliamentary secretary will tell us precisely what is intended to be done by way of regulations. The wording here reads:
Where a taxpayer has at any time ceased to carry on business or to be employed at the location or locations, as the case may be, in Canada, at which he ordinarily so carried on business or was so employed . .. and commenced to carry on a business or to be employed at another location in Canada-
A man who works in the northern end of Toronto, let us say, could be transferred to new employment, or find new employment in the southern part of the city, 20 or 30 miles away. Why should he not be able to claim moving expenses providing they are not paid for by the employer? These are some of the questions I wish to raise. If the parliamentary secretary has answers, we shall understand the bill a little better than we do at present. And we shall see where we go from there.

I should like to speak on clause 61, Mr. Chairman. I am particularly interested in the forward income averaging proposal. To begin, I should like to refer to the minutes of the Senate Banking Committee dated September 29, 1971, at page 3512. Mr. Stephen Smith, a witness before the committee, stated:
The more interesting one, really, is what is usually termed forward averaging. That is the provision in clause 61 which will be of most help to taxpayers who have a very high income in one year. Clause 61 permits the taxpayer to spread his income by taking any amount of his income and buying an income averaging annuity from an institution. He is given a deduction for the premium he pays for the annuity under certain limitations.
Speaking of the way in which the method would function, Mr. Smith said:
The annuity can be issued by any company authorized to carry on that business ... It must be issued for a single lump-sum premium . .. The annuity must be for life and with or without a guaranteed term, which cannot exceed 15 years.
While this might appear to be beneficial at first sight, I submit it has considerable drawbacks. I believe, also, that it is likely to have considerable repercussions upon the Canadian economy. Those who take advantage of this provision must buy an annuity which will pay a fixed amount for the balance of the years during which they live. Funds are tied up indefinitely in this annuity. This may not be a bad idea for persons approaching years of retirement. People aged between 50 and 65 might well wish to take advantage of it. But consider its effect on those of younger years, the restrictions it would impose on those who wish to change their positions, or businesses, who might wish to sell their property and expand their interests, and who need money with which to do it. It seems to me we could devise other types of forward averaging in connection with the so-called voluntary recovery appreciation which did not require taxpayers to put money into an annuity from which they could only draw a fixed amount each year.
It is often said that Canadians are great savers and investors in enterprises which carry no risk, but that they
November 1, 1971

are not good risk-takers and do not sufficiently support entrepreneurs. I would point out that those who are licensed to provide annuities are extremely restricted when it comes to the nature of the stocks and securities in which they can invest. The bulk of their investment is in government bonds and similar securities, so by means of this provision the government is in effect ensuring itself of a lending pool from which it will be in a position to draw funds. I question whether or not this provision is advantageous to the economy as a whole. I think we might well have to provide for alternative forward-averaging whereby the taxpayer would settle his accounts with the government, but within a shorter time than having to take an annuity that would span his whole lifetime. This provision might well affect significantly the pattern of borrowing and investment in Canada. If I am mistaken that the taxpayer must take an annuity for life at a set amount per year, then I shall be glad to hear the parliamentary secretary say so; but as I read the provision this is the only form of forward-averaging available and really locks in an individual for his lifetime. If someone is only 30 or 35, this may not be all that advantageous to the economy as a whole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Dauphin has misunderstood the provisions of this section. May I refer him to the definition of "incomeaveraging annuity contract" which appears at page 148 of the bill and is subsection (4) of section 61. This provision states that such an annuity may indeed be a life annuity, as the hon. member has pointed out, but subparagraph (B) also states it may be an annuity to the individual for a guaranteed term. So, the annuity can be of either type. If an individual chooses to average a lump sum payment over an eight or ten-year period, then he would buy an eight or ten-year endowment annuity. He also has the option, of course, to purchase a life annuity.
While I am on my feet, might I refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West? I see he has left the chamber, but since so many points have been raised I should like to mention this one before I forget it. The distance that a person has to move to get moving expenses is 25 miles. The distance is not governed by whether one moves from one community to another. In many of our cities such a distance could be traversed within the boundaries of the metropolitan area.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the parliamentary secretary whether there is a minimum time within which this forward-averaging annuity can be brought forward?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think there is a minimum time. If someone had a $50,000 payment and wanted to split it $25,000-$25,000, he could take a two-year annuity. But a taxpayer's own circumstances would dictate the option that he chose.

Mr. Chairman, this point has possibly been answered but it relates to section 56. Reference is made on page 129 to a retiring allowance, and I should like the parliamentary secretary to explain whether or not severance pay is included in this provision. There has been considerable anxiety about this on the part of many
Income Tax Act
people working in factories which close down and severance pay has either been negotiated or agreed upon, or in some way allowed. I wonder whether this provision relates in any way to severance pay.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, ordinarily severance pay is regarded as income under the Income Tax Act, and as such should be included in the computation of income. I am aware that in certain cases special regulations or legislation have been passed, but under the general income tax law this is regarded as income from an employment and is therefore included as taxable income in the year in which it was received. Again, of course, this is subject to the option of forward-averaging which we have just been discussing.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure members of the committee are all aware of the problems that may arise with severance pay. When a refinery closes down, any workers who receive severance pay are confronted with the fact that they cannot receive unemployment insurance since this pay is shown as earnings. The whole purpose of severance pay is to give people time to relocate themselves in some other part of Canada. This is a question that has received a lot of attention, particularly during the last two or three years.
According to section 62, which we discussed in this committee last week, in the event that a worker is told by Manpower to apply for a mobility grant for moving expenses, where would he apply? We have all heard of cases of people who have tried to obtain mobility grants under the manpower legislation, and section 62 does give consideration to relocation, moving expenses and so on. Would the parliamentary secretary elaborate on these two areas that are covered by section 62?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 56 carry?
Carried.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary would just clarify that point. That was the purpose of asking the question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not really in a position to discuss in detail Manpower mobility grants. If the hon. member can point to a section of Bill C-259 which brings them into income, then I will agree with him that these are taxable. If he can point to a section that excludes them from income, then I will agree they are excluded. But I am not entirely clear just what sort of comment the hon. member is expecting from me at this point.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot point to a section in this large volume before us. The only point I want to clarify is where the average taxpayer looks for assistance if he wants to relocate himself in some other part of the country. To which piece of government legislation does he look? Does he look to Manpower mobility grants or to section 62? When this question is placed on my desk, I like to be able to answer it. Invariably, of course, I have to telephone a department of government to find out who looks after what. This is the only point I want to clarify at this time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

Perhaps the minister in charge of these programs could elucidate a little more on what is to happen to these people and whether they will be involved under this new tax bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to appear obtuse, but I did think there was some general disposition to be relevant at this point. I seriously suggest that any discussion of manpower retraining programs at this particular time would not be relevant to the sections under consideration. I am sure the information the hon. member seeks could be obtained privately from the minister who is in the chamber at the moment. We have amendments to the Income Tax Act before us. The provisions in section 56(l)(m) provide that there shall be included in income amounts received by the taxpayer in the year as or on account of an adult training allowance paid to him under the Adult Occupational Training Act. That is about as far

as this particular bill goes in dealing with the subject the hon. member has raised. While I would not for a moment denigrate the remarks he has raised, and indeed I might be much happier discussing them than the bill before us, they are not germane to the present bill.

I feel they are germane to this particular bill because this is a new program announced on October 14, and these income tax matters will certainly have something to do with the incomes of certain individuals in Canada. While we are dealing with this matter a clearer explanation should be given as to what will happen to these people.

Mr. Chairman, I might agree with the parliamentary secretary that we are not considering things which come under other departments, but if he will refer to page 131 he will see that adult training allowances under the Adult Occupational Training Act are mentioned in this bill. Perhaps the analogy is not good, but the people of Canada are getting a little fed up with the number of departments of government in which there is no continuity. In this field of retraining we have manpower, labour and now income tax involved. We are trying to find out where these people should go to obtain the assistance to which they are entitled.
The parliamentary secretary suggests we are dealing with income tax matters this afternoon, but included in the bill are some things we want explained. We have a minister in charge of Manpower and Immigration, and perhaps he could give the explanation, but this matter of the Income Tax Act involves manpower mobility grants. These people involved in manpower mobility will be affected by these amendments and they are entitled to find out what they will mean. The parliamentary secretary would naturally suggest they should not go to the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Finance for that type of assistance, but perhaps he should indicate the department to which they should go. In all seriousness, I think this is a matter which should be explained to the people in order that they will know whether they are entitled to consideration under the Income Tax Act.
It is my feeling there are too many departments overlapping, all trying to build their own empires. No one in Canada seems to know where he is going or how to get there. Somewhere along the line there should be some continuity of purpose, so the taxpayer who is paying the shot will know which way to go and when.

Mr. Chairman, we could say that they are trying to play a trick on us, since the bill under consideration is against the small wage earner. Indeed, taxes throughout the world have always been paid by the rich or the lucky ones but under section 56, the poor would also be taxed. In my opinion, nobody now is in a worse position than the many unemployed Canadians and I wish to object to that clause, Mr. Chairman.
