speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, reference is made to bursaries at page 131 of the bill. Do I take it that a person in receipt of a bursary or scholarship is to be taxed to the extent that the value of it exceeds $500?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A person in receipt of a scholarship or bursary would be entitled to an extra $500 exemption over and above his personal exemption. The maximum would be either $500 or the actual amount of the scholarship or bursary obtained, if it happened to be less.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
It seems to me there is a conflict of aims or objectives. Obviously, the purpose of governments granting scholarships is to allow students who are non-earners to pursue their studies. If a student is an earner, the government would not be giving any bursary or scholarship. We give bursaries and scholarships at various levels of government in order that people in non-earning positions can continue to study and carry out research. I do not follow the logic of providing that a scholarship will not be taxed up to a value of $500, but only on the rest. A student could not pursue a course of study or hope to accomplish some objective in six to eight months on $500. If the exemption were set at a level which would permit a student to spend a year on his project, then it might make some sense.
It seems to me that this section treats the bursary as income and, therefore, assumes that the bursary is an earning. But it is not really. A bursary should not be regarded as an earning; it should be regarded as a grant given to a student to pursue some research which, in most cases, the provincial or federal government regards as a desirable objective. Or course, some students get grants from private sources, but if it is the opinion of the government that amounts from private sources are excessive, then this might be a reason for seeking to tax part of it in the hands of the private sources. If they think the amounts from government sources are excessive, then the obvious thing to do is to cut down the size of the grant from the government. But to tax above the first $500 of bursaries which are given to students to pursue studies and research does not add up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First, I must apologize to the hon. member for Portneuf for not answering his question immediately. I had to get the figures here. I have no idea of the number of individual taxpayers who might be involved. However, in terms of dollars, an estimate appears in the summary of the tax reform legislation, and I would refer the hon. member to page 64 of the English version. I hope it is the same page in the French version. I refer to the table entitled "Revenue Effect of Personal Income Tax Changes in the First Year of the New System". On the basis of the 1972 incomes, it is anticipated that the inclusion in income of unemployment insurance benefits would result in revenues of $130 million, while the deduction of unemployment insurance premiums paid by employees would result in revenue deductions of $100 million. So, the net figure is an estimated revenue gain of $30 million.
Income Tax Act
So far as the question of the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar is concerned, I did answer it at some length earlier this afternoon when the hon. member was unable to be with us. I shall simply say briefly that the thing to remember here is that this is an additional exemption over and above the $1,500 exemption, over and above the $100 standard deduction, and of course in addition to that students are entitled to deduct from their taxable income the amount of tuition that they paid to an institution. So, leaving aside the tuition completely, no student in receipt of a $500 or more scholarship or bursary would pay tax until his income reaches the amount of $2,100 a year. The $500 is not the level at which students start to be taxed, but it is an additional exemption over and above that which they otherwise have.
I would also take some exception to the hon. member's generalization that scholarships and bursaries are necessarily paid on account of need. Indeed, many are, perhaps most are, but certainly not all, and I think that is a fact to remember. I really feel that most students should not feel hard done by, by having to start to pay income tax at the level of $2,100 net after payment of their tuition fees for the year.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should shed some light on the argument that was started by the hon. member for Fundy Royal and which has been followed by others, winding up with the statement we just heard concerning the taxation of scholarships and the like. Having been a member of the committee, I may say that it was our feeling that if you added that to the basic exemption you probably got something that did cover tuition and residence fees of universities. I think that was the reason for it. Even so, I think a number of us did feel that perhaps we should not be so meticulous about bringing every dollar that moved in Canada within the clutches of the tax collector. We felt that there may be good reason for saying that students should have some kind of preferential treatment because we knew that later on, as the major taxpayers in Canada, from the preferred positions in the professions and with preferred income, they would be shouldering a substantial part of our income tax load. Anyway, I think the parliamentary secretary would probably agree with me that after the $500 which was arrived at, adding that to the basic exemption, you get $2,000, and we felt that generally this should be good enough at least to cover the university fees.
I should now like to go to another point, if I may. However, if anyone wants to follow up that line, I would be glad to yield my place for the time being.
Earlier today I made an objection to a story which appeared in the Mail-Star of Halifax on Saturday afternoon written by Dan Turner of the Canadian Press. I do not withdraw a word of the objection that I made to Mr. Turner's report as it was edited and as it appeared in that newspaper. However, he has shown me a report that he had apparently done earlier for the Canadian Press which I thought was eminently fair and which did represent what actually took place on Friday afternoon. I only wish the gentleman had carried that type of reporting forward into the next day. So, I have done him half an injustice, not a complete injustice, and he has done us a half injustice and not complete justice.

speechtext: I am not aware of any, Mr. Chairman.

I would like to put in a plug for the consideration of such. The government could offer incentive for companies to provide day care facilities on their premises. It could act as an example itself by setting up day care centres for its employees.
I think these remarks commend themselves. We are at the dawn of something that is very important.
My other point relates to the particular matter which I raised, namely the mama and papa position, that is the people who run the corner grocery stores or small businesses across Canada. Some of the provisions in the Income Tax Act simply do not give them tax relief. After I left the House on that particular evening, one of my colleagues mentioned a husband and wife who ran a garage under such circumstances-I guess you could call it a mama and papa garage. The wife brought their five children, under the age of six, who were placed in a room in the back part of the garage. They survived, I guess, as best they could through the day while mama attended to the books and so on and while papa attended to the job of dispensing the gasoline, grease, oil and so on.

This is similar to the situation I mentioned the other day where, because the business is not incorporated, such people do not get relief under the provisions of this act. Mr. Chairman, as you know, I have tried without success to persuade the government to exercise its moral and social conscience with regard to raising the exemptions of single individuals and married couples. I have also tried, without success, to change the government's view in respect of allowances for travelling expenses. I shall again try in my very humble way to persuade it to make certain changes in respect of other sections. I would direct the attention of the parliamentary secretary to page 129, of the bill which covers the question of alimony. If I read the section correctly, payments of alimony which have been made pursuant to either a court order or a separation agreement are not taxable income. A question arises in respect of a husband who pays moneys for the support of his wife and children and, because he does not have a court order or a legal separation agreement, cannot claim these moneys for income tax purposes. When I read this section I see the government is still sticking to the principle that there must be either a separation agreement or a court order before this amount is allowed as a deduction to the husband.
I would have thought from experience, and from the representations made by the various groups, the government might have yielded a certain amount and permitted as an exemption that payment by the husband to the wife for the support of herself and the children, even though
November 1, 1971

there is an absence of a court order or a separation agreement. We should keep in mind that in many of these instances where there is absence of either a court order or a separation agreement, the parties are motivated by one of two things. It may be that, because of religious principles, the wife is not motivated to move either for a separation agreement or a court order, or it may be that the husband is hoping for a reconciliation. However, why should he be penalized because, although he is assuming his family responsibilities and is making payments to his wife, he does not have a court order or a separation agreement. This strikes me as being unfair and inequitable. That is the first point I should like the Parliamentary Secretary to explain.
The second point is set forth on page 132 of the bill and is captioned "indirect payments". It reads:
A payment or transfer of property made pursuant to the direction of, or with the concurrence of, a taxpayer to some other person for the benefit of the taxpayer or as a benefit that the taxpayer desired to have conferred on the other person shall be included in computing the taxpayer's income to the extent that it would be if the payment or transfer had been made to him.
Quite frankly, I am not too sure what that means. Perhaps I might give an example. Suppose a husband and wife were separated and the husband was making a nominal payment to the wife but also held with the wife the mortgage on another property. Let us say the mortgage is in the amount of $10,000. As a result of some complaining by the wife that the amount he is paying to her is not sufficient he is persuaded, as a matter of moral social conscience, to transfer his portion of a mortgage to her which he had held jointly with his wife. Would this mean that the $5,000 in respect of the mortgage becomes taxable in the hands of the wife? If it does, there is something unfair about this provision. I may be misinterpreting this section, Mr. Chairman, and if so I would like the parliamentary secretary's assistance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Broadview was in his seat when I responded to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants on the problem of the reduction of total income to the family unit as a result of payments to one spouse by the other. Without going over that ground again, surely the hon. member will appreciate the problem raised in connection with alimony or maintenance payments by one spouse to the other in the absence of a court order or separation agreement. Some criteria have to be established in order to ensure that such payments are in fact made for the purpose claimed rather than simply as a device to avoid or reduce taxation.
The example which the hon. member cited in his discussion of section 56 (2) might be responded to in the same way. The payments covered by that section do not necessarily limit themselves to gifts as between husband and wife. The section is identical to present section 16 (1) of the Income Tax Act and its purport is to provide that amounts due to the taxpayer do not cease to be his income merely because he directs that they be paid to someone else. Other circumstances may enter into the transaction which would justify his suggesting that this should no longer be his income but that of the person to whom it has been assigned. However, the mere fact of assigning it does not relieve him of the liability for taxation on it.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the parliamentary secretary a question prompted by the question of my friend the hon. member for Broadview. The case is covered where there is a judicial decree or a legal separation drawn up in a law office and signed by both parties and witnessed. I do not see why it would be out of order if you had a simple written statement made by both parties to the effect that a sum of money had been paid during a taxation year for the support of one of the parties and the children residing with that party. This would not really be a written agreement of separation but simply an acknowledgement signed by both parties that one had paid and the other had received. Has that idea been scouted as a feasible way of tackling the problem?
Some people will not go to the expense of getting a divorce. I guess I got myself in trouble the other day by making a plea on behalf of some of them. Some people would go to a lawyer's office although they would not go near a divorce court. They are willing to try and regularize their legal liabilities. Some people prefer a simple way of doing things, just a sort of acknowledgement system. Has this ever been discussed?

speechtext: The section simply provides for a divorce, a judicial separation or a written separation agreement. This is a question of interpretation, which I would be glad to present to the Department of National Revenue for an answer. I should again point out that the jurisprudence should be ample here because this section is identical to one in the existing act.

Mr. Chairman, I should like further enlightenment because I was not satisfied with the answers given by the parliamentary secretary concerning the payment of alimony. We find that democracy has its limitations even though democracy depends on persuasion. It seems that no matter how much you attempt to persuade the government, it falls on deaf ears. It is rather unfortunate that we have run into this low state of democracy.
The other night I said, with all the strength of Horatio when he defended the bridge that fell, that I hoped some hon. members on the other side would come to the defence of some of the cases we have raised and would speak up and speak out in an attempt to persuade the government. an example, there is the problem of a couple I know who have a retarded child. The expenses incurred necessitate that both husband and wife work to make sufficient income to take care of that child and one other. I hope the government is not so callous as to disregard the expenses of a couple who are trying to meet their family responsibilities.
The miserable $500 allowed in circumstances like these is unworthy of any government. The example I have cited could be repeated many times across the country. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand that section 62 carried before six o'clock and that section 63 is the one we are now dealing with.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The reason I called section 62 was that it was not clear that the section had been carried. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre called it six o'clock and it was not clear whether it had been carried. If it was carried at six o'clock, then shall section 63 carry?
On clause 1-section 63: Child care expenses.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to have an opportunity of saying something on section 63 because this is a very definite, though small, breakthrough in a very important area, that of child care. I believe this is the first recognition by Parliament that has been given to the need for providing care for the children of working parents and I want to express my appreciation to the government for establishing this beachhead, as it were, in this particular area. I do not think, however, that this is a very big breakthrough, and I shall go on to say why. This is one of the gaping holes that exists in our social security system in this country. I am glad to see that a beginning is being made to plug this hole, though I think much more will have to be done to plug it thoroughly.
As I understand it, this section provides for a deduction of $500 for each child of working parents up to a maximum of four children, which is $2,000, or for two-thirds

November 1, 1971

of the parents' earned income, whichever is the lesser. At the outset I should like to put a question to the parliamentary secretary and he can either answer it now or make a note of it. I should like to know whether this deduction is applied to the total income of both husband and wife if both are working, or is it applied only to the lesser of the two incomes, be the lesser income that of the husband or the wife? Certainly this is not clear as the provision is now drafted.
We have to face the fact that conditions today are such that only a small number of working parents can afford to care for their children while they are away working. This may seem a startling statement to make, but as far back as 1965 when I was doing some door to door campaigning I was amazed at the large number of children who were out on the loose after school, with the front door of their houses locked or with a latch key around their necks and whose parent or parents were away working. This is far from the state of affairs that a good many of us think exists today that is, parents looking after their children at all times during the day. Many people think that if parents are away working, relatives care for the children. But we have now moved almost imperceptibly to the point where there is no one to care for so many of these children, be they relatives or neighbours, unless special arrangements are made.
For a long time many people were worried that there was no federal provision-or any other kind of provision for that matter-to plug the gap that was left when the mother or father, or both, were working away from home during the daytime. To substantiate my statement that only a minority of working parents can afford to take care of their children while they are away, I should like to cite some figures. Admittedly, these are not 1971 figures but they are the latest I could obtain. They were compiled by the women's bureau of the Department of Labour.
According to these figures, in 1966 the median annual earnings of working mothers were $1,783-that is, working mothers with husbands-and $2,856 for widowed, separated and divorced mothers. This last category embraced 10 per cent of the mothers in the working force. I think the figures prove the point I am making, namely, that on these salaries or wages working mothers simply cannot afford to look after their children by paying others to care for them adequately.
The women's bureau also said that 29 per cent of families of working mothers where the husband was present had a combined annual income of less than $6,000 in 1966, and the average combined income for a two-parent family was $7,302. One might suggest that since 1966 wages and salaries have gone up. That is true, but I want to point out that the cost of living has also gone up enormously since that time and that the situation has become even more aggravated.
Proof of what I am saying lies in the fact that when the Royal Commission on the Status of Women was hearing representations and visiting many parts of Canada this was the problem expressed above all others, that is, the urgent need for child care for parents working outside the home, particularly for working mothers. That royal cornincome Tax Act
mission was impressed with the urgency of this matter. I should like to point out the need from another angle.
Again using information supplied by the women's bureau of the Department of Labour, a survey was conducted in April of 1967 which showed there were 540,000 mothers of children under 14 years of age in the labour force. One working mother in every five had children under 14 years of age. This involved more than one million children. The other day I asked the women's bureau to make an estimate of the current figures and they came out with the following: as of July 24 this year, instead of 540,000 mothers in the labour force with children under 14 they estimated there were 678,000 working mothers with children under 14. Almost 20 per cent of the mothers in the labour force have children under 14 years of age.
This is a very serious situation, one which shows that the time is long overdue to help working mothers with child care arrangements. The problem is growing and it is divided into a number of categories. The after school problem is very serious. When we complain about vandalism, juvenile delinquency and all that sort of thing we must realize that a great deal of it is the result of lack of proper and adequate arrangements for children coming home after school when the mother is out working. This would also apply in respect of a father of a single-parent family.
This summer I attended a conference in Ottawa on child care. It was attended by representatives from across Canada. At that time I realized this problem is growing worse by leaps and bounds in every province. I also attended a single-parent conference recently in the city of Ottawa and discovered that in a great many families the father is the only parent to care for the children. This adds to the difficulties.
The problem is most acute and urgent in respect of children under school age. In 1967 there were 357,000 children under six years of age whose mothers were in the labour force, yet less than 3,000 of them had been placed in day nurseries or centres. The need today is much greater and is growing fast. The Royal Commission on the Status of Women said there should be 450,000 places in child care centres provided in the immediate future.
For a few minutes let me refer to the element of cost of child care facilities. Under this income tax bill a deduction of $500 is being allowed per child, up to four children, or a total of $2,000. One hon. member from Toronto indicated the other day that this figure fell far below the actual cost of child care today. I have discussed this cost with child care people and have come to the conclusion that $500 is a very unrealistic figure in relation to the actual cost of child care.
The $500 deduction works out to $10 per five-day week in a 50-week year, or $2 per day. I should like to know if any member of this House knows where you can get child care for $2 a day. If I did know I would be hustling around to get the minimum wage people working on the situation. This is a very low figure which the government is providing. The amount of $2 per day for child care is pretty mean and also represents a violation of the federal minimum wage laws.
The actual minimum for which child care can be provided is $15 per week. This works out to an annual figure

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act
of $750. There are very few child care centres where you can obtain child care for $750 a year. The actual minimum market figure begins at $20 a week, or $1,000 a year. That is exactly twice the figure provided for child care in this legislation. It would be a very good idea for the government and the Parliamentary Secretary to have another look at this figure. The Canadian Conference on Child Care this summer suggested that even $1,000 per year was a minimum starting figure and that the actual market price was considerably higher.
Let me suggest also that this problem is far too big to leave to private arrangements. I may have to come back to this matter a little later because I see I have just about exhausted my time on the first round, so I will confine myself at this stage to private arrangements. I think the government is thinking in terms of parents making their own child care arrangements with individual baby sitters. That is a very unrealistic situation. Even if the exemption were raised to $1,000, which is far more realistic, this situation would not be good enough.
We have reached a stage when we must consider child care as we consider education. Years ago education was left to parents who had the means to hire private tutors or send their children to private schools. Only the well-to-do could afford that. There were tutors and private schools available for them, but we came to the conclusion in Canada many years ago that this system was not good enough for the people of this country. I think the government will have to go much further than even $1,000 a child. This is a realistic starting figure; it should be at least $1,000 per child per year instead of $500. The government, however, will have to go much further than that. I will leave the matter at this point and return to it later.

Mr. Chairman, before making a speech I should like to ask a question of the parliamentary secretary. How did the government arrive at the figure of $500 in respect of this exemption? It might be interesting to know how it was arrived at. Is it a ball-park figure, or what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one unnamed colleague here just mentioned, that is a mysterious process. The process by which these figures are arrived at involves a combination of things that are fed into an assessment of what the revenue impact may be and what objectives one would like to achieve in making changes to the Income Tax Act.
In this particular case the estimated revenue reduction as a result of the child care allowance we are talking about is $50 million a year. In all these figures such as rates, exemptions or any other deduction which may be limited by a top figure, for example, the employment expense allowance, we try to strike a balance between the government's revenue requirements and what we would like to do both politically and equitably for the taxpaying public.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on this provision. I do not profess to be an authority in this area such as is the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. However, I have spoken to individuals who have had to deal with the problem. I was
(Mrs. MacInnis.J
a little surprised to find out what is being paid to baby sitters these days. It seems to me that the "grandmother figure" who looked after children as I knew the situation does not work for peanuts any more but works for union wages.
One even hears about people putting children through college by looking after someone's youngsters. I was horrified to hear the charges made for looking after children. I suppose this might be fairly natural for a bachelor because he is not accustomed to paying these costs. If one were in the position of being a single parent it would seem to me it would be almost cheaper to get married. Seriously, it seems to me we should consider a larger exemption for people who have to contend with this problem. We already find that within new apartment complexes day care centres are being established. With this type of exemption such centres may be more widespread.
When both parents work they have the problem of providing care for their children. It is logical that some arrangement should be made for the children quite apart from the convenience to the parents. In this connection I am very interested in the welfare of the children. If a single parent should be involved, or if both parents are involved because they must work for economic reasons, I think the child has a claim on society for a proper upbringing. I am quite concerned when I hear of people who are unable to provide an adequate standard of living for their children. In some cases the solution to this problem may mean the provision of baby sitters or day care centres. I think we should consider an increase in the $500 exemption because of the problems which people have.

Mr. Chairman, there is one point I wish to raise. I am going to strike out for male liberty in respect of this provision. Many people have been talking about single parents and there has been a suggestion that it is always the mothers of children who are involved. This act does not provide for the father at all except if he should be separated from his wife pursuant to a written separation agreement. This is repeated time and time again in the act. A man can qualify for the child care allowance for his children only if he is no longer married, second, if he is living separate and apart from his wife pursuant to a written agreement or, third, if the wife is certified by a qualified medical practitioner to be a person who by reason of mental or physical infirmity is confined for a period of not less than two weeks to an institution.
How about widowers?

The widower is not specifically provided for, nor is the man whose wife decides she wants to play in greener pastures and has left him with children. We know this happens. Perhaps it does not happen quite as often as the case of a husband deserting, but there are many instances in which the wife deserts and leaves the children with the husband.
It seems to me the separation of these parties should be wider than pursuant to a written agreement. The widower, of course, is covered by the provision that he is not married since under these provisions he is not considered to be married. I must say there are many instances in which the wife has deserted the husband and has left the children with him. He would be in no position to negotiate
November 1, 1971

an agreement, nor would there be a compelling reason to do so.
Perhaps a court order should be included. Suppose the parties were separated merely by means of a court order: say, for instance, that the family court decides for the benefit of the children or for other reasons that the husband shall live separate and apart from the wife. If the children are in the custody of the husband, surely to goodness he should be entitled to receive the child care allowance. One provision which might be abused is the deduction referred to in section 63 (l)(b) (iii)(A) where the wife may be confined to bed, there is a certificate that she is so confined for a period of two weeks, and there is need for child care. I think something could be worked out under that provision.
I ask the parliamentary secretary why the benefit is restricted to the taxpayer who is the father of children and who is separated pursuant to a written agreement. I know there might be opportunities for the parties to decide to live apart in order to see if they can get some edge. But surely to goodness where it is proved that the wife has decamped, or where a court has ordered the parties to live apart with the husband having the care and custody of the children that should be sufficient for him to qualify for the child care allowance.

Mr. Chairman, there are three questions that I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary at this point. The first concerns the matter of receipts. What will be the position of full-time university students who work during the summer to earn money to cover university fees and who require day care for their children during the university year? Under the act will they be recognized as parents working in the home?
The next question is, what will be the position with respect to receipts which must be submitted as validation for claims, first in the case of established day care centres? What will be the process for validating these organizations? The second case is with respect to parent co-operatives. What legal entity exists in a parent co-operative, because they would be issuing receipts to themselves?
Having said this I should like to deal with the matter of the receipts. This matter has been one of the more thorny issues among the people with whom I have discussed the question. There is the point of view that it is a pretty good thing to issue receipts because in this way some kind of standard is established. This is why I want to find out from the parliamentary secretary what the validation process will be and generally what the criteria for these receipts will be. It seems to me that if there is child care and receipts are issued for it some kind of standard should be required in connection with the child care. A very dubious benefit will be conferred on the child if we do not have some criteria in this respect.
Another point which I wish to raise is that a number of low income people with whom I have talked would like, to look after children and get paid for doing so under this income tax deduction provision, but they are afraid that if they do so this would interfere with their social assistance and, as a result, their social assistance might be cut.
Income Tax Act
Therefore I took the trouble to contact the Canada Assistance Plan people in the National Health and Welfare department and found out that if you are fortunate enough to live in some provinces you may receive $500 for looking after someone else's children without social assistance being reduced. The provinces wherein one's social assistance would not be reduced are Ontario, Quebec, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and British Columbia. Nova Scotia is close to the line but it would probably be on the right side of it. In the other provinces social assistance would be affected before you could get $500 for looking after children. This is something which the parliamentary secretary should consider. He should find out whether there is some way in which this matter could be handled by his department in co-operation with the social assistance authorities, because it is a real problem for people on social assistance who want to become engaged in child care work.
There is another point which I should like to mention. When payments are made to people for child care there should be some obligation regarding the quality of child care. I do not know whether the parliamentary secretary would like to answer all those questions at this stage, but I would like to pursue the matter of eligibility and criteria if he would answer them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The question which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked first in her first presentation was whether child care allowance was applicable to the total income of the family. The answer is no. As to whether it is applicable to the lower of the two incomes, again the answer is not necessarily, although in practice that would be the usual case.
Section 63 makes it very clear that if the lady in the house is earning an income she is automatically qualified to claim this, but the man in the house has to pass a number of tests in order to be able to claim it, as was alluded to by the hon. member for Edmonton West. Either they are separated or he is not married and is supporting children for one reason or another, being a widower or divorced, or his wife is separated from him pursuant to a written agreement, or his wife is mentally or physically incapacited for a period of time during the year which would permit him to claim this allowance under section 63.
In passing I might refer to the comments of the hon. member for Edmonton West and note that of course in this particular area in almost every circumstance that I could conceive which the hon. member mentioned, the taxpayer would be entitled to claim a full, married exemption on behalf of a dependant other than his wife if the circumstance which he described existed. I would like to look at his comments to see if by any chance we have provided a situation where a man could not claim either the child care deduction or the married exemption on behalf of a dependant other than his wife. However, I do not believe that that situation exists. I think he is entitled to one or the other in those circumstances.

What if he puts the children in a boarding school and avails himself of the provisions governing the placing of children in a boarding school, with its limitations? He would be denied that?

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not think so. Assuming that his wife is not claimed as a dependant, one way or another he would be able to claim the equivalent of a married exemption in respect of one of the children. He would be able to claim the child care allowance up to $15 a week for the boarding school and up to the limit of $500 per child and $2,000 for the family. This is the sort of thing that I would like to pursue with the hon. member over a cup of coffee, when we could get down to the particular section in the bill in some detail. But I believe I am correct in my interpretation.
The questions raised by the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway in her last presentation regard, first, the university student. The answer is yes, the university student can claim this exemption provided he can say that the child care payments were made for purposes of earning income and not simply for purposes of freeing the parent to attend university.
The exemption during the year is related to the earning of income and I would think that in many cases the working university student, one who works during the off season, would find that he or she could in fact claim at least a good part of this $500 exemption during the period that he or she is earning income. The allowance is not there specifically to allow the university student or any other student to claim the exemption so that he can attend the institution of his choice. It is related to the earning of income.
On the matter of day care services, there is no special restriction on this as far as the co-ops or anything else is concerned. Someone must issue a receipt; that is the whole situation. There should not be any problem about a parent co-op if it is bona fide and if it issues a receipt.
Earlier today we discussed the problem which arises when we propose to allow people to make a deduction from their taxable income in respect of payments made to people living under their own roof, to people within the family unit. In equity to the general body of taxpayers it is felt that some provision should be made to circumscribe and formalize the arrangement whereby a taxpayer can reduce his taxable income by making payments to another person in the family. As the hon. member can appreciate, these payments can be made to other members of the household provided that person is not entitled to be claimed as an exemption by the taxpayer claiming the child care allowance.
Undoubtedly there will be some administrative inconvenience for the taxpayers concerned, but we hope that the benefit of the general allowance, which will be a matter of an additional $50 million left in the hands of the taxpayers for the coming year based on the 1972 income, will outweigh any administrative inconvenience.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary mentioned administrative inconvenience. That raised an important question in my mind which I shall pose as briefly as I can. What sort of thrust is there for change in our income tax law within the Department of Finance and also the Department of National Revenue which perhaps has the more immediate responsibility for administering the law?
I ask this question because as we get into a whole new system of reforms it is possible that we may create as many injustices as existed under the old system against which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and others fought for so long. Earlier today the parliamentary secretary said that people were burning the midnight oil in order to try and solve the problems. Perhaps the problem I chose was an unfortunate one because it has been around for years and has not yet been solved.
We have passed a good many reforms today and I hope that somewhere we get credit for that. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could tell us how the process of reform works within the administration. Perhaps if we understood that we would feel better about saying "adopte".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a private Member of Parliament I suppose that from time to time I feel as strongly as does the hon. member about the frustrations encountered when making representations to the Department of National Revenue on behalf of constituents whose cases seem transparently equitable at first blush. I must agree that we are into a period where the Department of National Revenue will be called upon to deal with a number of new situations. There are under this bill many new concepts being created for which there is no jurisprudence and no backlog of judicial or administrative decisions for guidance.
Speaking for the minister of the department that establishes tax policy, as opposed to that which administers the tax law, I can only say that we have attempted to achieve in the new tax law and the bill a situation of tax equity, and that applies not only to the relative treatment of different taxpayers but also to the relationship between taxpayer and the Department of National Revenue. We hope and intend that the Department of National Revenue will deal with this new tax bill in a fair, reasonable and realistic way. We expect that they will because we believe they are competent to do so and have the same objectives in mind. This is something which will be proved over a period of time. I can only give a testimonial in advance. I hope I can give the same testimonial three or four years from now.

Could I ask a further question? I understand that a few months ago the Minister of National Revenue had established a group of people from across Canada who would advise him on an informal basis. I know the man from my own area is Professor Edwin Harris. I have complete confidence in him and I am sure the other people were chosen were equal care. I should like to know if it will be the responsibility of that particular group to consider any complaints that we may have about the operation of this new law a year from now when people have had a chance to see whether it has worked well.
How do we get to that group? Do we funnel our inquiries through the minister, or may we direct them in any other way? Will the group be carrying on continuing studies to ensure that we do not have to go through the great exercise in which we have been engaged for ten years and also to ensure that tax reform may come about more quickly in the future?

November 1, 1971

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the problem is in the area of administering what this Parliament presents to the Minister of National Revenue to administer, then the avenue suggested by the hon. member of dealing through the minister and his advisory council is correct. On the other hand, if it turns out that we have misconceived here what we thought we were doing, and if a change in the law rather than a change in the method of administering the law is indicated, then representations should be directed to the Minister of Finance.

I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could tell us what Solomon-like distinction has been imposed upon blood relationship. At what point does the distinction cease? At page 153, lines 38 to 40, section 63 (3) (a) (iii) (B) reads:
who, during the year, was under 21 years of age and connected with the taxpayer or his spouse by blood relationship, marriage or adoption-
Perhaps there is a definition clause, but I have not been able to find it. Is blood relationship to be limited to immediate family? Is it the niece, nephew, great aunt? Do we get as far as great aunts? With many of my good Chinese friends anybody who is of the same family is known as cousin or auntie. Some of these relatives are joined by marriage. Why, in those shorter periods when the spouse is confined to hospital, shall we say, for an illness, is the sister-in-law being eliminated? I ought to mention a younger sister-in-law. She may be the most convenient and logical person to hire as a baby sitter; she knows the children. Yet the act seems to insist that one should get an outsider. Why is there this elimination?
I know some people say, "You will get your mother-inlaw in to look after the children and she should not be entitled to qualify as a satisfactory child care attendant." I am just wondering why you should eliminate, say, a sister-in-law, the wife's aunt, or other persons bearing a similar relationship. I should be interested to know what is the thinking of Solomon in this connection.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: And here speaks Solomon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will not attempt to answer the first part of the hon. member's question except to this extent: I refer him to section 251. If after perusing that rather lengthy section that deals with arms-length transactions, the definition of arms-length and the definition of persons related by blood relationships he is still in some doubt as to the clarity of the section, I would be glad to answer. These matters are defined in section 251.

But, Mr. Chairman, the term arms-length connotes a different relationship and serves another purpose. An arms-length transaction is a business transaction and implies a business relationship. Here we are talking about child care allowance. Are we to lay down lines as to blood relationships?

Is the hon. member talking of anyone in this House?
Income Tax Act

No, I am not talking of anyone in this House. It is remarkable that language like this should be used because there are such things as kissing cousins, and so on. They bear a second cousin relationship, which is a blood relationship and comes within the banned limits so far as marriage is concerned. Why would there be that sort of restriction with regard to the child care allowance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry the hon. member wants to debate this question before looking at section 251 which deals with arms-length transactions. Actually, I am sorry that I said what I did because obviously my remarks led the hon. member to misunderstand what I said. The section also defines a number of other relationships, including those he mentioned and about which he asked a specific question. As I said earlier, I could read subsection 6 of section 251 which defines blood relationships for the purposes of the Income Tax Act, if that would help. However, the hon. member may wish to look at it himself. If he has some particular questions about the section, he could raise them now.
On the question of a sister-in-law and her eligibility for payment in respect of the child care allowance, I do not think that under section 63(3)(a) there would be any real problem so long as it is clear that the relative, be it a sister-in-law or otherwise, is not a person whom the taxpayer claiming the deduction is also claiming an exemption for under the Income Tax Act. I think the payment could be made to anyone who is actually performing the service.
The only problem arises when payment is made to someone who during the year was under 21 and who is connected with the taxpayer by blood relationship, adoption or marriage- in short, who is a person whom the taxpayer might claim as an exemption or claim an exemption in respect of for the year. I do not think there is any real problem so long as it is not a person with respect to whom the taxpayer was entitled to claim an exemption.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should leave discussion of this section without mentioning that, important though this provision is, if this is the government's whole program in regard to child care-and there is no indication that there is to be anything more-it is not adequate at all. We have gone past the stage when many people can provide through their own means for adequate child care arrangements. The commission appointed by the government went deeply into this matter and suggested that we cannot get by in this regard unless the federal government takes the initiative in providing for proper child care in co-operation with the other two levels of government. The federal government should take the initiative, it is recommended.
I raise this matter at the present time because there seems to be no other clause in the bill under which I can discuss it. The omission I refer to should be included in one of the sections. May I ask the parliamentary secretary if consideration is being given to the idea of a child care program in which the federal government will assume, not only the 50 per cent of operating costs allowed with respect to child care centres under the Canada Assistance Plan but also the 70 per cent of capital costs in connection with such projects for the initial seven-year period as

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act
recommended by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. It suggested that the federal government's assumption of such charges is essential in the matter of child care.
I hope we are not just talking about the idea of baby parking, or about the aunt, grandmother, niece or other relative looking after the baby while the mother is working. I hope we are talking about modern knowledge as to how young children of under school age must be treated and dealt with to enable them to develop fully. Modern thinking and teaching on this subject says that we need day care centres for working mothers in a variety of locations. In some cases we need them in the community, in others in the factory and in some cases in homes where there will be adequate training, proper supervision, and so on.
I do not think we should get the idea that the $500 deduction from income tax contemplated in the section will do much to provide an adequate child care program across this country. It will not. Even if this provision led people to look after their children from the financial point of view, it still would not provide what is required for children or for the development of children across this country. It will not provide for Canada the sort of thing that is being provided in many countries of the world where children are taught under expert guidance, with helpers in child care centres so that growth, development and habit formation are promoted.
I know that much of what I have just said is not directly relevant to this section. It is, however, extremely relevant to child care. In my opinion, before this session ends the government ought to let us know that it is going ahead with a child care program across this country which will include a provision such as this one relating to the deduction of income tax and which will also enable the provinces and municipalities to set up day care centres where children of working mothers or working parents can be looked after. I think that is what the government ought to be considering at this time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suppose that the adequacy and timing of any particular government program is always open to criticism. As to who was right and who was wrong, that is something the historians will be better able to judge than those of us who are on the scene right now. I agree with the hon. member and appreciate her concession that this is indeed a significant step forward and a significant breakthrough. Hopefully, I feel it will be more adequate than she evidently feels it will be. Of course, that remains to be proved.
In response to the general proposition that the hon. member has posed regarding day care centres, whether I agree with her or not is rather irrelevant. Today we are talking about the Income Tax Act-concessions, deductions, exemptions and allowances, that may be made under that act. In the context of Bill C-259 we are not talking about whatever positive initiatives the federal government could or should be taking with regard to the establishment of this type of program in Canada.
I respectfully invite the hon. member to direct her ire, interest or whatever it may be to the Minister of National

Health and Welfare when he is next in the House. All I can talk about is income, deductions from it and the tax that is imposed on the balance. In that context we have taken a very significant and meaningful step forward in terms of child care allowance and recognition of the fact of the working mother in our society.

Mr. Chairman, I was somewhat disturbed by reading section 58. I hope I am in order in discussing the section. I understand we are dealing with this group of sections. It came to my attention only a short while ago. If I understand the section correctly, it seems that it is in effect a repudiation of contracts entered into in the 1920s and 1930s.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am inclined to agree with your ruling. Mr. Chairman, the clause under discussion can be best described as a mini-care provision for children, brought forth by a mini-minded government. When one looks at the contents of the provision, a miserable $500 for child care, one realizes the inadequacy of the amount. The parliamentary secretary stretched out his chest to its full extent when he said this program would cost the government $50 million on the basis of a $500 exemption. I remind him that the cost of refitting the Bonaventure was $18 million and the cost of building the elite Arts Centre in Ottawa was $46 million. I remind the parliamentary secretary that our budget for national defence each year is almost $2 billion. The miserable $50 million that he claims the government will lose as a result of the $500 exemption is really small potatoes compared to the total picture.
I am very happy that the Minister of Justice is in the chamber this evening. He will appreciate the impact of this miserable $500 allowance for child care. He knows the best type of law we can implement is preventive law. When young children are left unattended after school, they get into real trouble. This is when they develop into delinquents, graduate into young offenders and, finally, criminals in the full sense. The blame rightly can be placed on parents who do not have the money to take care of their children during working hours. To allow only $500 to working parents who require the money they earn to keep the family together is shortchanging them. It is developing a situation that can work hardship with regard to the children and the problems they have.
November 1, 1971

I hope the Minister of Justice, in his rosy, persuasive way will recommend to the parliamentary secretary the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that the minimum amount should be at least $1,000. This amounts to $20 a week, or $4 a day for child care services. The hon. member pointed out that $500 a year amounts to $2 a day for child care purposes. If we are going to save money on crime prevention and increase the prestige and reputation of the Minister of Justice in this very important field, he will see what I am driving at with regard to child care services. I hope he will persuade the likeable Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance that the appropriate amendment to make the allowance $1,000 should be brought forth.
What is $100 million when we take into account some of the larger problems we face with our young people? The Minister of Justice had a very difficult time trying to justify the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act. I hope he will see that young people, not only in the province of Quebec but in every province of Canada are given proper child care so that they can develop into good, decent young Canadians. Although I do not speak with the eloquence of the Minister of Justice when he is in full flight, I speak with humility and, I hope, persuasiveness. I hope he will persuade the parliamentary secretary that the minimum amount should be $1,000.

Mr. Chairman, when I rise to speak I always have the assistance of those people who are not in the House but are drinking coffee behind the curtain. I would like to echo the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and the fact that this exemption is a step in the right direction. However, I think it is a timid step. The hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand said it is a short step. My hon. friend from Broadview said he was humble, and I agree that he is humble. Some people say he has every right to be humble. He says he is the most humble person in the House of Commons.
What has that to do with the bill?

The only thing he is arrogant about is his humility. I support the contention of my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kingsway on the basis of the exemption of $500 per child. It is a step in the direction of providing some assistance for parents who are working, and I think increasingly in our society in order to earn a decent income both parents must be out of the home.
That is one of the glaring failures of our economy. The stresses in our society which result from this kind of situation are something I do not think we can tolerate much longer. If they are required to work to maintain the middle-class standard we often see displayed on television, we must do something about the casualties of their union, the children.
My hon. friend from Broadview mentioned the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice has just attended a session in Ottawa called Poverty and the Law. It pointed out, among other things, that among the unemployed poor and also the working poor there is not equal access to justice in our society and there is developing in our legal system a specialized association to deal with this particular problem which is a poverty problem.
Income Tax Act
Now the parliamentary secretary can snigger. I do not know whether he is concerned about this. I looked him up in the Parliamentary Guide before I came down here. The Parliamentary Guide says the parliamentary secretary has all the assets of a Chamber of Commerce man par excellence. He even mentioned this. Here is a man who is on the board of directors of many interesting establishment corporations and he has been very successful in his business life. I am not envious of this. It is suggested here that there is something immoral about this particular parliamentary secretary because he has made a lot of money. I do not agree with that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member may be able to convince the Chair that he is being relevant to the section under discussion. I invite him to do so.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the only thing relevant about my last few remarks is that it might be said they were relevant to attacking the parliamentary secretary. I will desist, however, because if you look over his words in the last few days and in the last week and note his responses to some of the questions, and read them back to him, where he failed to answer a lot of serious questions which have been raised and ran around and hid, I think the Hansard will attack him and I do not need to continue on that line.
My contention is that there is a great need for day care centres which will not necessarily be aided and abetted by the incentive offered. In my own constituency we have a number of kindergartens and day care centres. I will tell you who goes to them. It is not the children of the working poor and of the unemployed. The children who go there are the children of doctors and business and professional men who can afford to send their children there, not because their wives are working but because they would prefer to go somewhere else.
What we need is a system which would allow the children of these people who have to be absent from home the kind of enrichment all of us know, especially our Minister of the Environment, the kind of enrichment which is provided to young children by these day care centres properly organized and properly led by trained teachers, which is not available to people who do not have the kind of affluent background which can provide the experience so necessary to learning.
I would say that compared with the affluent in our society the working poor and their children suffer almost as great a cultural gap, and that affects their learning, as exists between the working poor and our native people. This is how serious it is. If I may be free to enlarge on that topic for a moment I would like to say this, because it happens to be a field in which I have at least some professional competence. In our society, learning is largely verbal learning or learning through the printed word. Children from homes with little in the way of written material, little in the way of cultural enrichment do not have the background which is necessary for them to succeed in the verbal skills which are required in order to succeed in school.
By the time they reach grade three they get what is known as an IQ test which is based on verbal learning. When they receive this, because they do not have the background they are labelled with a low IQ for life. As

November 1, 1971
Income Tax Act
they move through the grades, the gap widens. We are denying a whole segment of our society, because they lack those particular skills, the kind of advancement which is available to the parliamentary secretary and to the hon. member for Fraser Valley West.
When I argue for the development of day care centres and properly run kindergartens, if you like, or playschools, I want them to be available to families or children who really need them, because there is a cycle in poverty, a cycle in being on welfare and the only way in which we can break this cycle is to develop the kind of aptitude which can best help a child who comes from a home which is economically disadvantaged. We should provide such help for the children who really need it.
So I am in agreement with my hon. friend from Van-couver-Kingsway and my hon. friend from Broadview that we should establish a system which will not leave a child in the hands of the poorly trained girl next door or the kindly grandma but will develop through income tax exemptions a system which is well run and which would be led by well trained people.
By God, we have many people in our society, well trained ones, who are not doing anything. It is not that we do not have jobs for them today. That is not the point. The main point I should like to make is that the $500 exemption is not enough. The average person who is earning $5,000 a year or below spends $500 on putting his child in an adequately run school. I think it should be raised at least to $1,000 because the future of our leadership, the future of our whole society, democracy, if you like-if I do not sound too pretentious, presumptuous or anything else-depends upon an electorate which is intelligent and has an equal opportunity in society.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is the understanding of the Chair that pursuant to special arrangement made last Friday, the committee will now move to the consideration of a grouping of sections 117 to 120 inclusive, together with sections 146,147 and 204. Shall section 117 carry?
On clause 1-Section 117: 1972 rates.

Mr. Chairman, earlier today I inadvertently stumbled into this field. I took advantage of one of the small sub-sub-sub-clauses to section 56 or 57 which dealt with income tax averaging, but I will not continue those remarks. They dealt with the problem of why one would take advantage of certain circumstances when one's income was on the rise but not when one's income was on the fall. I used the name of a hockey player, and perhaps I should have not done so because Mr. Gordie Howe, the man I referred to, always had a rise in income until he saw he was at the end of the trail and rather sensibly decided to get out before he started to go backward. For the rest of the day I have frantically tried to think of other sporting figures who did not follow the sensible example of Mr. Howe but stayed on until it was too late for them, but oddly enough I could not think of any specific examples though I have read about dozens in the world of baseball.
In any event, the problem we are faced with is that the averaging provisions that have been presented to us were spawned in a time of inflation, and perhaps this is why the government has presented these averaging provisions in the bill. The parliamentary secretary said, and I think rightly, that the House of Commons committee struggled with the question of downward averaging but simply could not come up with an acceptable formula. That is true, but this does not mean that we cannot come up with an acceptable formula though it does mean that no one yet has. I think we will do an injustice if we pass this on to the ballplayer or sporting figure or the artist we are trying to help, people who are going over the hill and find themselves going down the down staircase instead of up the up staircase.
That philosophical observation out of the way, I hope we will yet come up with a better formula. After all, Joseph in Egypt was able to mingle seven fat years with seven lean years and come up with something that averaged itself out, and perhaps this is the sort of example we should follow. Having said that, may I ask the parliamentary secretary why section 117(8) is now being struck out? It appears on page 312 and was new. It is now being discarded.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with my hon. friend from Halifax-East Hants. We regret that we have not been able to find a suitable way to deal with downward averaging. It was said earlier today that this was a problem that the parliamentary committee dealt with at length and neither it nor its advisers were able to find an answer. Nor were we able to locate any other jurisdiction that had been able to resolve the problem satisfactorily. This does not mean that we ought not to continue the
November 1, 1971

search. I quite agree that we should and I can assure the hon. member that we shall.
The provisions in section 117 are the rate schedules that tie in very distinctly with the exemption schedule discussed under section 109 a number of days ago. I think it should be noted that they do carry out the commitment, over the period between the taxing years 1972 and 1976, that the Minister of Finance gave to reduce the rate of personal income tax on the first $500 of taxable income from the 17 per cent that will be in effect next year down to a 6 per cent level in 1976. This, of course, is one of the provisions that executes the government's undertaking that the tax reform measures now before the House will not be measures of tax increase in disguise.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary secretary indicated a moment ago, section 117 sets out the rate schedule. In other words, it specifies the rate at which each taxpayer will have to pay tax on the first $500 of his income, then on the next $1,000 of his income, and so on up as far as it goes. The parliamentary secretary has already pointed out that built into section 117 is an arrangement whereby these rates make at least a modest decline over the period of the next few years.
However, I should like to come straight to the point of my intervention at this juncture. We are not satisfied with many things about this rate structure. As hon. members are aware, we do not accept the philosophy of the government that has resulted in a reduction of the rate on the top increment, bearing in mind that at the same time the government is doing away with federal estate tax and also bringing in a capital gains tax that is applied to only 50 per cent of income that is defined as a capital gain.
However, our concern throughout this debate on the income tax legislation has been and continues to be for those in the lower income brackets. We further contend, bearing in mind what you have ruled from the chair we can do, that there should be a reduction in the rate of tax applied to the first $500 of taxable income.
Possibly, I am making a mistake I made once before by giving my procedural points before moving the amendment I have drafted, but I think you and I, Sir, will agree that the ground has been pretty well cleared. You have made it clear that there are certain types of amendments you and those associated with you at the table feel you cannot accept. On the other hand, you have made it clear that if a private member moves an amendment to reduce a rate of tax and if that reduction is across the board- and you will recognize, Sir, I am using your own words- and if there is no transfer of the incidence from one group of taxpayers to another, Your Honour feels that type of amendment is acceptable.
You made that statement to one of my friends in the Social Credit Party when he sought to move one of that group's amendments. You made it again when the hon. member for Regina East moved an amendment to reduce the figure having to do with income tax deductibility in respect of medical expenses. Then again on Friday of last week, when I made another unsuccessful attempt to move an amendment having to do with another feature of the
Income Tax Act
tax bill Your Honour said to me that if it were a reduction in the rate, if it were applicable across the board to all taxpayers, Your Honour would, of course, accept it.
I hope you appreciate how easy I am making your chore in this instance. I have already said that apart from any thoughts we might have about the rates of tax in the upper brackets, about the estate tax, the capital gains tax and so on, we think that the tax payable on the first $500 of taxable income should be a lot less than it is. As long as the exemption level is where it is we think there should not be any tax at all in that bracket. Of course, we cannot raise the exemption levels. We have tried and we have been ruled out of order in our attempts.
I submit it does fall to us that we have the right to move that the rate of 17 per cent which is specified in line 30 on page 305 be reduced to a lesser figure, and that is what I propose to do. Once I move to reduce that figure of 17 per cent to a lesser percentage that, of course, results in the necessity of making a reduction of the same number of dollars in each of the succeeding paragraphs.
If Your Honour is now looking at page 306 you will see that on that page each paragraph starts with an amount which represents the aggregate income tax up to that point and then indicates the rate of tax on the next increment. I have no intention of proposing any juggling of the rates or any attempt to increase the rate at one level to make up for it at another. I am proposing exactly what Your Honour has said is our right, namely, that there be a decrease in the rate on the first $500 of taxable income. Having moved for a reduction in the rate on that first $500, I then propose that the same number of dollars which that reduction produces for everyone in that first category be taken off each of the other figures all the way up from paragraph (b) to paragraph (m).
Having described my amendment, the moving of it is a mere formality. I have it here and I admit that it is in my own handwriting, but I have several copies of it and I trust it is legible. I move:
That Bill C-259 be amended, at pages 305 and 306, by changing the figure "17 per cent", in line 30 on page 305, to the figure "2 per cent", and consequentially by reducing the amount at the beginning of each of the paragraphs (b) to (m), both inclusive, on page 306, by $75.
I could have written that amendment in a longer form by taking each of the paragraphs on page 306 and actually saying that the $85 in paragraph (b) be reduced to $10, and that the $175 in paragraph (c) be reduced to $100 and so on down the page. But rather than produce such a long and wordy amendment I thought it would say the same thing if I simply said in my amendment that the amount at the beginning of each paragraph on page 306 be reduced by $75.
As Your Honour realizes, the effect of this amendment is one that is clearly across the board. It reduces by 15 percentage points the rate of taxation on the first $500 of every taxpayer's taxable income, whether he is a taxpayer who has only $500 of taxable income or whether he has $100,000, or what have you. The amount of reduction, by the same token, becomes the same for the person in the upper brackets as it is for the person in the lower brackets, namely, 15 percentage points of the first $500-in other words, $75 across the board. There is no cumulative effect to it and there is no increase in the reduction for
