those in the upper brackets. There is just as much of a reduction for the $500 person as there is for the millionaire, and I point out again that there is no shift of the incidence. I might mention that there are none of the things that Your Honour found procedurally wrong in some of the previous amendments. Therefore I have the pleasure of presenting this amendment and perhaps I might read it again. It is:
That Bill C-259 be amended, at pages 305 and 306, by changing the figure "17 per cent", in line 30 on page 305, to the figure "2 per cent", and consequentially by reducing the amount at the beginning of each of the paragraphs (b) to (m), both inclusive, on page 306, by $75.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has urged some very persuasive arguments and authorities on the Chair and I am inclined to agree with him. Some of the observations the Chair made previously may have been obiter, nevertheless I think the hon. member is correct in his argument that under our rules a private member can move a motion to effect an across the board change reduction in rates of taxation as long as they do not affect the incidence of taxation. I am prepared to accept the motion unless there are arguments that would dissuade me.

Mr. Chairman, of course it is a very interesting move the hon. member has made here. In fact he has done what the government has refused to do. He has applied a form of tax credit which would be the kind of flexibility a government could move into if the income tax were fixed in amounts in relation to the brackets and not the percentages, and if there were changes to be made in particular brackets then the particular credits could be made.
As Your Honour has indicated, the amendment is acceptable to the Chair. I would suggest the Chair look at subsections (2), (3) and (4). I have never heard of negative income tax being accepted in this House, and the acceptance of this amendment would result in some most interesting circumstances as a result of the further subsections which apply to tax in the years 1973, 1974 and 1975. There would be negative income taxes in the low income brackets. That is a matter for the Chair to ponder.
I would point out that we are looking at only the rates of the federal tax, but there is a little thing called the provincial tax which goes with this. These schedules, on the basis of subsection 1(a), give the tax for the year 1972. They indicate the tax rate on the income in the bracket and then, of course, we have the combined federal tax and the 30 per cent provincial tax. The schedules as shown in the act indicate the federal rate for 1972 and also the combined federal-provincial rate on the assumption that the provinces will levy a tax equal to 30 per cent of the federal tax rate. For instance, in the first bracket it would be 17 per cent plus 30 per cent of 17 per cent, or a total of
22.1	per cent.
This will effect some change in the federal share of the income tax but, of course, it will have no direct result on the quantum of the provincial tax, which is something many people have failed to recognize. I want to indicate that the House committee which studied the proposals on the white paper came down with some very definite

recommendations concerning the level of tax on the federal side which is generally accepted in these proposals.
Much has been said about the tax being lowered to 50 per cent or less at the $60,000 level. But if you throw in the 30 per cent provincial income tax the total levy goes up to 61 per cent. For instance, at $60,000 the federal tax at the beginning of the bracket is $21,795. The federal tax rate on the income in the bracket will be 47 per cent, but combined with the provincial tax this means that those over $60,000 will be taxed at 61.1 per cent. That is the flat rate right now. The province of Manitoba goes as high as 39 per cent. So it will be 39 per cent of 47 per cent. That will add up to a fair amount, much higher than it is in, say, the province of Ontario.
But let us look at the middle income group, the group between $9,000 and $14,000.1 might point out that many of the friends of the hon. member to my left are in that group. One does not have to go very far today to get in the bracket of $11,000 to $14,000. First-class constables and firemen, in some areas, are in this bracket. This applies to first-class constables in a number of cities in this country. Then there are members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as well as others. The total tax rate in the bracket between $11,000 and $14,000 will be 40 per cent. Now we will see who starts screaming at the levels of income tax as a result of these changes which are proposed.
I also wish to point out something else. There has been a significant change in structuring federal personal taxation. Under the existing system the federal rates imposed contain room for an abatement in respect of provincial taxes, and in addition there are imposed separate taxes for old age security and social development. All these things are being lumped together. They are being called a new standard federal rate which does not provide for standard provincial abatement. Any tax levied by the provinces will be in addition to the federal rates. The only specific exception in the bill is a deduction of 3 per cent of the portion of tax otherwise payable that is related to income earned in a province providing schooling allowances. That means the province of Quebec.
It also seems likely that further abatements may be made on a basis similar to that under the established programs, the Interim Arrangements Act, for provinces opting out of certain shared federal-provincial programs. It is possible, but we will see what comes out of the conferences this week and early in November. At present Quebec is the only province which has so opted and an abatement of 19 per cent of the tax otherwise payable applies in respect of Quebec income.
At the present time a 28 per cent standard abatement is allowed. I spoke of a 30 per cent abatement for illustrative purposes but that does not mean the provinces are bound in any way by this, because whereas at the present time there is a 28 per cent standard abatement, Manitoba actually levies a 39 per cent tax and Quebec levies its own personal tax.
Therefore we must come to the conclusion that these rates are in themselves exceedingly high. As a matter of fact, when you consider that an individual who earns $60,000 pays $28,000 income tax on the $60,000-that is, right at the start-he pays just under 50 per cent on
November 1, 1971

average. Remember, when we say a 61 per cent tax rate on income in the bracket, that is a marginal rate and in actual fact the total tax is just under 50 per cent.
If one were to take the income group between, say, $9,000 and $14,000 and figured out for them the average tax payable, one would see that a person who is earning about $10,000 would be paying about 25 per cent of his income in income tax, right across the board. Add to that his sales taxes, his customs duties and his share of other taxes-I will put aside any question of property tax-and we will see just how much tax the individual is paying.
We are complaining about the quantum of money that is taken from the individual because somebody has made it popular and it has now grown into the philosophy that Big Brother government knows better.
Hear, hear!

Big Brother government is motivated by my hon friend and his pals. They know better how to do item I am talking about the average individual who should be able to decide far more than he does how he earns and how he spends his money. Of course, I can take the hon. member's argument all the way and say, "Take everything away from the individual, give it to the government and let the government spend everything or keep it."
Who said that?

That is an extension of the argument. If Big Brother government knows better how to spend the money, then it is logical to pursue it all the way through and to give the government all the money so it can be spent to the best advantage. If the hon. member's argument has any strength whatsoever, surely that is the natural conclusion. It seems to me that in many instances that philosophy underlies most of their stands.
Are you for or against it? Make up your mind.
I am not particularly in favour of this amendment.
You are against the people.
I know the hon. member has made up his mind and therefore anything anybody else says is superfluous. He has the humility of the man who has made up his mind and will brook no other views.
Let us have some humility from you, Marcel.

That is all I want to say about this particular subject. We note the changes that are to follow. The amendment does cause a problem there. Possibly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has further amendments which will follow, but he has not indicated them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Does the hon. member realize that if this amendment carries, it follows that there should be amendments to the other subsections and I shall have them at that time?

It does not necessarily follow, but in any event that is the position with regard to these items.

Mr. Chairman, for the last couple of days we have been trying to impress upon the Canadian public the advantage of a tax credit system as against the exemption system and tonight, in a very bold, dramatic and highly intelligent amendment the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has shown how it should be done. The value of the amendment before us enables us to grant tax relief to those in the lower income brackets without accelerating the process and providing substantially more advantage and relief to those in the higher income brackets.
It is very difficult to demonstrate the value of the tax credit system as against the exemption system in the normal course of trying to explain it, but this amendment illustrates how it can be done. While the government has had difficulty in trying to figure out an intelligent approach to providing relief for those in the lower brackets of the income tax level, the hon. member has shown them the way, I hope they will seize his torch and accept the amendment before the House.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

I shall try to give an honest answer in three minutes, Mr. Speaker. The decision to rehabilitate the Glace Bay plant owes much to the initiative of Premier Regan. The previous Nova Scotia government had sought federal financial assistance but wanted to retain control of the rehabilitation program; the federal government had replied that it would only be prepared to provide such assistance if the province assigned responsibility for the operation of the plant to a concern in whose competence federal authorities would have confidence.
Premier Regan has now proposed that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited should take on responsibility for both the rehabilitation and the operation of the plant until such time as the earnings from production have repaid the federal costs. This proposal was attractive to the federal
November 1, 1971

government but before replying an up to date estimate was required in order to determine whether the rehabilitation of the plant was technically feasible and, if so, at what cost and on what time scale. This was the engineering survey assigned to AECL as announced in January, 1971. AECL concluded that the plant could be rehabilitated and that this could be done more quickly and at less cost than would be involved in building a new plant at some other site.
Further study was nevertheless required in order to determine whether by the time the plant could be rehabilitated there would still be a continuing requirement for its production of heavy water. This additional point has now been thoroughly investigated and it has been established that there will be a continuing requirement for the output of the plant.
During his recent visit to Halifax the Prime Minister Mr. Trudeau, was in a position to announce that agreement had been reached. AECL will acquire a leasehold interest in the Glace Bay plant and will assume full responsibility for its reconstruction and eventual operation. The necessary funds will be lent by the federal government to AECL, to be repaid with interest out of sales of heavy water once the plant is in production. The lease of the plant to AECL will terminate upon completion of that repayment.
I am delighted, Mr. Speaker, that this long standing monument to the incompetence of a previous Nova Scotia government is now being renovated, for the betterment of all Canadians. Additionally, some 300 to 400 job opportunities will be opened for Nova Scotians in the course of the work which will commence by the end of this month.

It is well known that Indians on reserves, as well as inmates of penitentiaries, are presently excluded from the count of employed and unemployed persons. This exclusion is not only discriminatory, it is also incomprehensible because the federal government is allegedly trying to bring our native peoples up to the standards of well-being enjoyed by Canadians generally. I say "generally" because a large number of Canadians are out of work.
The money the federal government has been spending in its drive to help the native population may or may not have been well spent.
